templates.title: Watermark detection outcomes — files with all, part or none of the watermark, per content type, detector version and week
templates.subtopic: latest row per key with DISTINCT ON, tie-breaks, FILTER, NULLIF shares

sections.scenario: A research lab publishes a detector that checks whether an image, video, audio clip or piece of text carries an imperceptible watermark added by its generative models, and reports an outcome with a confidence level. The same file is often checked several times, sometimes by a newer detector version. The reporting team publishes a weekly summary per content type and detector version: how many distinct files carried the watermark throughout, in part, or not at all, with low-confidence results shown apart so they never inflate either side. Only outcomes are stored: a file is known by a hash, and no content is kept. The outcome categories and confidence levels are this exercise's rule; check current docs for any real detector.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over detection_checks that returns week_start, content_type, detector_version, files, watermarked, partial, not_watermarked, low_confidence, watermarked_share, one row per (week, content type, detector version) that has at least one file, ordered by week_start, content_type, detector_version. A file's result for a detector version is its latest check by that version (latest checked_at). The file then belongs to the week (Monday start, UTC, as a date) of that latest check. files counts the files in the group; low_confidence counts those whose result has confidence low; watermarked, partial and not_watermarked count the outcomes of the other files only. watermarked_share is (watermarked + partial) / (files − low_confidence) rounded to 3 decimals, NULL when no file in the group has a result above low confidence. {{week_rule}} {{error_rule}} {{tie_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). check_id is unique but not in time order. The sample has {{checks}} checks; a public detector receives far more, so say how your query would scale.
sections.assumptions: Content types, detector versions, outcomes, confidence levels and counts are synthetic. The detector's internals are out of scope: this is reporting on outcomes it already produced. The data was extracted after the last week ended.
sections.criteria: One result per file and detector version, chosen by checked_at with a deterministic tie-break; errors excluded before choosing; the week of the latest check; low-confidence results counted apart and kept out of the outcome columns and the share; NULL share with no confident file; correct rounding; deterministic order; sound answers on cross-version reporting, incremental maintenance and small groups.

clarifications.q: A file was checked on Tuesday and again on Thursday by the same version. Which result counts?
clarifications.a: Thursday's, the latest. The file counts once.

clarifications.q: The same file was checked by two detector versions.
clarifications.a: It has one result per version and counts once in each version's row.

clarifications.q: The latest result is low confidence, but an earlier one was high.
clarifications.a: The latest stands: the file counts only in low_confidence.

clarifications.q: A file was checked on Sunday and again on Monday.
clarifications.a: It belongs to the week of its latest check, Monday's week, and nowhere else.

clarifications.q: What if every file in a group is low confidence?
clarifications.a: The row still appears, with zero in the three outcome columns and a NULL share.

hints: Reduce to one row per (file, detector version) first: DISTINCT ON (file_hash, detector_version) … ORDER BY file_hash, detector_version, checked_at DESC, ….
Decide what to filter out before choosing the latest row, not after: a row you filter after DISTINCT ON has already hidden the one you wanted.
Aggregate with COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …), and divide with NULLIF(…, 0) cast to numeric before rounding.
followups: Product asks for the share of files with any watermark per content type, across versions. Which version's result should a file contribute, and why is adding the per-version rows wrong?
A new detector version rolls out over two weeks. How would you report the files where the two versions disagree, without keeping any content?
At hundreds of millions of checks a week, how would you keep this report up to date incrementally when a file is re-checked days later?
A partner wants per-day numbers for one content type with a small volume. What would you publish, and what would you hold back so that rare files cannot be singled out?

rules.ask: MAX gives you the latest time, but how do you fetch that check's outcome and confidence, and what happens when two checks share that time?
A file was checked three times by the same version. How many times does your query count it?
check_id is not in time order. Show a file where the greatest id is not the latest check.
Where in your query is the error filter: before or after you pick the latest check? Walk through a file whose latest check is an error.
Which check's timestamp decides the week for a file checked on Sunday and again on Monday?
What does your share return for a group where every file is low confidence, and why?

templates.title: Confidence bands in a protein structure release — residue shares per organism, and predictions mostly in the lowest band
templates.subtopic: band classification with CASE, two-level aggregation, residue-weighted shares, de-duplication

sections.scenario: A public database of predicted protein structures gives every prediction a per-residue confidence score from 0 to 100, and its documentation groups the scores into four bands so readers know which parts of a structure to trust. Before a release, the data team checks each organism's predictions: what share of all residues falls in each band, and how many predictions are mostly in the lowest band and need a clear warning on their page. This exercise uses its own band edges; check current docs for the database's. It is a data check only: nothing here draws any biological or medical conclusion from a prediction.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns release, organism, predictions, residues, very_high_pct, confident_pct, low_pct, very_low_pct, mostly_very_low, one row per (release, organism) with at least one prediction counted, ordered by release, organism. This exercise's bands, by plddt: very high at 90 or above, confident at 70 or above and below 90, low at 50 or above and below 70, very low below 50. predictions counts the organism's predictions in the release; residues counts their residues. Each _pct is 100 × residues in the band / residues, over all the organism's residues in the release (not an average of per-prediction shares), rounded to 1 decimal. mostly_very_low counts predictions with strictly more than half of their own residues in the very low band. {{release_rule}} {{null_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). plddt is NUMERIC(5,2), so a value can sit exactly on a band edge. The sample has {{predictions}} predictions and {{residue_rows}} residue rows; a full release has hundreds of millions of residues.
sections.assumptions: Accessions, organisms' predictions and every confidence value are synthetic; accessions use a made-up format. Band edges and the "mostly" rule are this exercise's rule; check current docs. Residue numbering starts at 1 within each prediction.
sections.criteria: Inclusive lower band edges; residue-weighted percentages over the whole organism and release; "mostly" as strictly more than half of a prediction's own residues; withdrawn predictions excluded where present; unscored residues kept out of every count and duplicate rows counted once at Very Hard; correct rounding; deterministic order; sensible answers on fragments, changing band edges and scale.

clarifications.q: Which band is a score of exactly 70.00?
clarifications.a: Confident. Each band includes its lower edge.

clarifications.q: Should the organism's percentage be the average of its predictions' percentages?
clarifications.a: No. Count residues across all its predictions in the release, then divide.

clarifications.q: A prediction has exactly half its residues below 50. Is it mostly very low?
clarifications.a: No. Strictly more than half.

clarifications.q: An accession appears in two releases.
clarifications.a: Each release is reported on its own; it counts once in each.

clarifications.q: Can the four percentages fail to add up to 100?
clarifications.a: Yes, by rounding. Do not adjust them.

hints: Classify each residue once with a CASE on plddt, using >= on the lower edges, in a CTE.
Aggregate twice: per prediction (its band counts and its residue count, for mostly_very_low), then per release and organism from those counts.
Divide as numeric (100.0 * …) and round only the final value.
followups: Long proteins are split into overlapping fragments, each its own prediction. How would you report an organism's residue shares without counting the overlap twice?
The documentation changes a band edge in a later release. How do you keep the old release's report reproducible and comparable?
The release has 200 million predictions. How would you compute this check, and which parts would you precompute when the residue files are written?
Readers want a per-residue confidence track on each entry page. What would you store per prediction so the page loads fast, and how would you keep it consistent with the bulk download files?

rules.ask: Two predictions of 10 and 1 000 residues. What does an average of their shares say about the organism, and what does the residue-weighted share say?
Which band does your query give a residue of exactly 90.00, and what does the exercise's rule say?
A prediction has 6 of its 12 residues below 50. Is it mostly very low in your query?
What exactly makes two residue rows duplicates, and what would your query do if a re-delivered row carried a different score?
An unscored residue: is it a residue for the denominator, for the "mostly" half, both or neither in your query?

templates.title: Reruns that did not reproduce — same config, code, data snapshot and seed, but a different final metric, per project and month
templates.subtopic: composite keys with NULLs, FIRST_VALUE or ROW_NUMBER, tolerances, month bucketing

sections.scenario: A research lab's experiment tracker records every run: its project, config hash, code version, data snapshot, seed, start time, final status and final metric. Re-running a run with the same recipe should give the same result, within a small numerical tolerance. Each month the reproducibility working group reviews the reruns that did not reproduce, per project, to find nondeterminism before it reaches a published result. Every run, metric and project here is synthetic.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query over runs that returns month, project, reruns, not_reproduced, max_abs_diff, one row per (month, project) with at least one rerun, ordered by month, project. A recipe is the combination of project, config_hash, code_version, data_snapshot, seed. Only runs with status completed and a final_metric count. The first run of a recipe is its earliest such run by started_at; every later one is a rerun. A rerun did not reproduce when abs(final_metric − first run's final_metric) is strictly greater than {{tolerance}}. month is the first day (a date) of the UTC month of the rerun's own started_at. reruns counts reruns, not_reproduced those that did not reproduce, and max_abs_diff is the largest absolute difference among the group's reruns. {{month_rule}} {{edge_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). final_metric is NUMERIC(8,4): compare it exactly, never as a float. run_ids are assigned in start order. The sample has {{runs}} runs; a tracker holds millions.
sections.assumptions: The tolerance, projects, hashes, code versions, snapshots, seeds and metrics are synthetic; what tolerance is right for a real metric is a judgement this exercise leaves out. A run's recipe never changes after it starts.
sections.criteria: Completed runs with a metric only, filtered before choosing the first run; the recipe as all five fields; reruns compared with the first run, not the previous one; strict tolerance in exact numerics; the rerun's own month; deterministic tie-break on start time; NULL seeds excluded rather than grouped together at Very Hard; deterministic order; good answers on per-project tolerances, diagnosing causes and incremental maintenance.

clarifications.q: A rerun differs from the first run by exactly the tolerance.
clarifications.a: It reproduced. Only a difference strictly greater than {{tolerance}} counts.

clarifications.q: Do I compare each rerun with the run before it, or with the first?
clarifications.a: With the first completed run of the recipe.

clarifications.q: The first attempt of a recipe failed.
clarifications.a: Failed and cancelled runs never count, as the first run or as reruns. The first completed run is the first run.

clarifications.q: The same config and code ran with a different seed. Is that a rerun?
clarifications.a: No. A different seed or data snapshot is a different recipe.

clarifications.q: Which month does a rerun belong to when its first run was in the month before?
clarifications.a: The month of the rerun's own started_at.

hints: Filter to completed runs with a metric first, then find the first run per recipe with FIRST_VALUE(final_metric) OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY started_at, run_id) or ROW_NUMBER.
A row whose ROW_NUMBER is 1 is the first run; every other row is a rerun.
Think about what PARTITION BY does with a NULL in one of the key columns.
followups: Some nondeterminism is expected (for example, non-deterministic GPU kernels). How would you let a project declare its own tolerance, and keep this report honest when a project sets it very wide?
The working group wants to know which part of the recipe to suspect. What extra fields would you record per run, and how would you report reruns that differ only in hardware type or library versions?
A recipe has fifty reruns with a bimodal metric. Is "compared with the first run" still the right definition? Propose another and say what it reports.
The tracker holds millions of runs. How would you maintain this report incrementally as runs finish, including runs that finish out of start order?

rules.ask: A recipe's metric drifts by half the tolerance on each rerun. What does comparing with the previous run report after four reruns, and what does the rule ask for?
A rerun differs by exactly the tolerance. Does your query count it as not reproduced?
Two runs have the same config, code and snapshot but no recorded seed. Does your query treat them as the same recipe?
Two runs of a recipe started in the same minute. Which is the first in your query, and is that deterministic?
Where in your query do failed and cancelled runs drop out: before you choose the first run, or after? Walk through a recipe whose first attempt failed.
Why compare NUMERIC metrics exactly here, and what could a float comparison do to a difference equal to the tolerance?

templates.title: Pareto front of runs — the runs no other run beats on both accelerator-hours and score
templates.subtopic: skyline (Pareto front) by one sort and a running best, tie groups

sections.scenario: A research team runs a sweep of training runs and wants to show, on a run-comparison page, the runs worth looking at: those that no other run beats on both cost and quality. Cost is accelerator-hours (lower is better) and quality is an integer evaluation score (higher is better). Every run, hour and score here is synthetic; the page only compares numbers the tracker already holds.
sections.problem: Implement pareto_front(runs). runs is a list of (run_id, accelerator_hours, score) records in any order, with integer hours and scores. Run A beats run B when A's hours are at most B's, A's score is at least B's, and at least one of the two is strictly better. Return the ids of the runs that no other run beats, ordered by accelerator-hours ascending, then by run_id ascending. Two runs with the same hours and the same score do not beat each other: both are kept. Return [] when there are no runs. {{score_rule}} {{relog_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 80 000 runs in the timing check, most of them on the front. Comparing every pair is O(n²); keeping the front as a list and checking each run against all of it is O(n·f), and both are too slow when the front is large. O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Hours and scores are synthetic integers. Only these two numbers decide the front; the page shows the other fields of a run but they play no part here.
sections.criteria: The correct beats relation with equal pairs both kept; one sort plus a running best handled per hours group; output ordered by hours then id; [] for no runs; at Hard, unscored runs ignored, zero hours allowed and None for negative hours; at Very Hard, the last record per run id; O(n log n) with a clear argument; good answers on a third objective and live updates.

clarifications.q: Two runs have the same hours, and one has a higher score.
clarifications.a: The higher score beats the other.

clarifications.q: Two runs have exactly the same hours and score.
clarifications.a: Neither beats the other; both are on the front unless a third run beats them.

clarifications.q: How should ties in the output order be broken?
clarifications.a: By run_id ascending, as strings.

clarifications.q: Is a run with fewer hours but a lower score beaten?
clarifications.a: No. It is better on one and worse on the other.

clarifications.q: May I raise an exception for bad input?
clarifications.a: No. Return None in the cases the statement names.

hints: Sort by hours ascending. A run can only be beaten by a run that comes before it or shares its hours.
Process one hours value at a time: within a group only the top score can survive, and it survives when it is strictly above the best score of every cheaper run.
Keep that best score as a single number while you scan.
followups: Prove that your scan keeps exactly the runs no other run beats, including equal pairs.
A third objective (peak memory, lower is better) is added. What happens to the one-sort approach, and what would you do for 80 000 runs?
Runs finish one at a time and the page must update live. Which structure keeps the front so that each new run is inserted or rejected in O(log f)?
The team wants the runs within 1% of the front, not only on it. How would you define that, and compute it?

rules.ask: How many comparisons is that for 80 000 runs, and roughly how long in Python?
Most runs in the timing check are on the front. How many comparisons does checking each run against the whole front make?
Sorting by score first can work too. Which tie rule on hours do you then need, and why?
Two runs share hours and score. Walk through your comparison: does either remove the other?
A run is logged twice and the second record has no score. Is it on the front in your code?

templates.title: Dividing a compute budget by max-min fairness — whole accelerator-hours, nobody above their request
templates.subtopic: max-min fair share (water-filling) by one sort, integer remainders, tie rules

sections.scenario: A research lab shares a quarter's research compute among projects that each request a number of accelerator-hours. When requests exceed the budget, this exercise's rule is max-min fairness: small requests are met in full, and the rest of the budget is shared equally among the larger ones, in whole hours. The allocation is published to every project, so it must follow the rule exactly, including where the last few spare hours go. Every project, request and budget here is synthetic; how a real lab allocates compute is not described.
sections.problem: Implement allocate_hours(requests, budget, prefer="id"). requests is a list of (project_id, hours_requested) in submission order; budget is a whole number of hours. If the budget is at least the total requested, every project gets its request. Otherwise let L be the largest whole number such that giving every project min(request, L) fits in the budget. Every project gets min(request, L); the hours left over are fewer than the projects whose request is above L, and go one each to those projects in the order prefer names. Return (project_id, hours_allocated) for every project, in input order. Return [] when there are no projects. {{prefer_rule}} {{invalid_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 50 000 projects and budgets of billions of hours in the timing check. Handing out one hour at a time is O(budget) and out of the question; capping one project per round and recomputing the share is O(n²) when requests are staggered. O(n log n) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Projects, requests and budgets are synthetic. Allocation is in whole hours. A project never receives more than it requested, and hours nobody requested stay unallocated.
sections.criteria: Requests at or below the level met in full; the largest level that fits; spare hours fewer than the uncapped projects, given in the named order; output in input order; at Hard, prefer="smaller", zero requests, budgets of 0 or above the total, and None for negative input; at Very Hard, repeated projects merged at their first position; O(n log n) with exact integer arithmetic; good answers on weights and redistribution.

clarifications.q: Can a project end up with more than its request?
clarifications.a: Never. A project whose request is below the level gets exactly its request.

clarifications.q: After equal shares there are 2 hours left for 5 uncapped projects.
clarifications.a: They go to the first two of those projects in the order prefer names; the others get none of them.

clarifications.q: Does a capped project take part in the spare hours?
clarifications.a: No. Only projects whose request is above L.

clarifications.q: Which order should the output be in?
clarifications.a: The input order of the projects.

clarifications.q: May I raise an exception on bad input?
clarifications.a: No. Return None in the cases the statement names.

hints: Sort the projects by request. Walk through them, keeping the budget still to share and the number of projects still to serve.
If the smallest remaining request is at most an equal share of what is left, it is met in full; otherwise every remaining project is above the level, and divmod gives you L and the spare hours.
Sort only the uncapped projects by the prefer order to hand out the spare hours.
followups: Prove that the L you compute is the largest level that fits, and that no project could get more without one that has no more getting less.
Projects now carry weights (a priority from a review). How does the sort-and-walk change for weighted max-min fairness?
Mid-quarter, two projects return unused hours. How would you redistribute them without changing anyone's allocation downwards?
The allocation is published to every project. What would you publish with it so that each project can check its own number?

rules.ask: The budget is about 8 billion hours. How many loop iterations is that, and how long would it take?
Each round you find the smallest request and recompute the share. How many rounds for 50 000 staggered requests, and what does each cost?
Your rounds cap every project at or below the share at once. How many rounds can that take, and can you prove it stops?
Hours are whole numbers. Where can a float division give one project an hour too many or too few?
You sort by request. How do you still return the projects in input order, and how do you break ties for the spare hours?

templates.title: Residue contacts in a predicted structure, at an exact cutoff
templates.subtopic: 3D cell lists of cutoff-sized cubes, exact integer distances, sequence separation

sections.scenario: A public database of predicted protein structures offers each prediction as a file of atom coordinates with a confidence score for every residue. Many people who download the files compute the same thing first: the residue contacts, the pairs of residues that sit close together in the predicted fold although they are far apart along the chain. The data team wants to ship a contact list with every entry in a derived bulk download, so that nobody has to recompute it, and the list must be exactly reproducible: the same file and the same cutoff always give the same pairs. The first entry to check is {{structure}}. Each residue is represented by one atom whose coordinates are given in thousandths of an ångström, as integers.
sections.problem: Implement residue_contacts(residues, cutoff, min_conf=0). residues is a list of (residue_number, x, y, z, confidence) tuples, one per residue, with x, y, z the integer coordinates of the residue's representative atom in thousandths of an ångström (they can be negative) and confidence an integer from 0 to 100. Residue numbers are unique. cutoff is a positive integer in the same units. Two residues a < b (by residue number) are a contact when both are counted, b - a >= 3, and the squared distance between their atoms is at most cutoff * cutoff: the boundary is inclusive and exact. A residue is counted when its confidence is at least min_conf. Return every contact as a tuple (a, b), each pair once, sorted by a and then b. Return [] when there are none. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check is a compact synthetic globule of 50 000 residues (far more than one chain, so that the cost shows) about 296 ångströms across, with an 8 ångström cutoff. Comparing every pair is 1.25 billion distance checks. Sorting by x and scanning forward while x is within the cutoff does not save you here: in a compact fold every slab one cutoff wide still holds about 1 300 residues. Something close to O(n + contacts) is expected.
sections.assumptions: Structures, coordinates, confidence values and cutoffs are synthetic. Which atom represents a residue (often the beta carbon, or the alpha carbon for glycine), the cutoff and the confidence floor are this exercise's rules; check current docs for how contacts and confidence are defined and used. The contact list describes geometry only: nothing here draws a biological, medical or clinical conclusion from a prediction.
sections.criteria: Exact integer comparison of squared distances with an inclusive boundary; the separation rule by residue number, at least 3; residues below the confidence floor left out with all their contacts at Hard and Very Hard; gapped, unordered numbering handled at Very Hard; each pair once, sorted; negative coordinates bucketed correctly; a cell list (or a k-d tree argued carefully) close to O(n + contacts), with a clear argument for why the slab scan is still quadratic on a compact fold; sensible answers on batch runs, several cutoffs and comparing model versions.

clarifications.q: Is a pair exactly at the cutoff a contact?
clarifications.a: Yes. Compare dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz <= cutoff*cutoff in integers; no square roots, no floats.

clarifications.q: Why leave out residues fewer than 3 apart in the chain?
clarifications.a: Neighbours along the chain are always close because they are bonded to each other, so they say nothing about the fold. In this exercise b - a must be at least 3, counted in residue numbers.

clarifications.q: Can coordinates be negative?
clarifications.a: Yes. The origin is arbitrary, and a structure can sit on both sides of it.

clarifications.q: Is a residue exactly at min_conf counted?
clarifications.a: Yes. Only residues below it are left out, and every contact they were part of goes with them.

clarifications.q: What if two residues are listed out of order, or numbers have gaps?
clarifications.a: Only at Very Hard. Separation is always by residue number, never by position in the list.

clarifications.q: What do I return for a structure with no contacts?
clarifications.a: An empty list.

hints: Two atoms within the cutoff can be at most one cutoff apart along each axis. Which residues can never be partners of a given one?
Put every counted residue in a cube of side cutoff, keyed by (x // cutoff, y // cutoff, z // cutoff) in a dict. A residue's partners are in its own cube or one of the 26 cubes around it.
To check each pair once, compare a cube with itself and with 13 of its 26 neighbours (one of each opposite pair). Python's // rounds down for negative numbers too, which is what the keys need.
followups: The contact list must be computed for every entry in a release, hundreds of millions of residues in all. How would you run it as a batch job, and how large is the output?
Users want contacts at several cutoffs, from 6 to 12 ångströms, from one pass. How would you size the cubes, and what would you store?
A new model version changes some predictions. How would you report, per entry, the contacts that appeared and disappeared, and what would you say about contacts between low-confidence residues?
Contacts between two chains of a predicted complex are needed too. What changes in the input, the separation rule and the output?

rules.ask: How many pairs are there at 50 000 residues, and how long does that take at about ten million comparisons a second in Python?
After sorting by x, how many residues share a slab one cutoff wide in a fold about 37 cutoffs across? What does that make the cost per residue?
Why must the cube side be at least the cutoff? What would you have to change if you made it half the cutoff?
What does building and querying the tree cost here, and how do you make sure a pair exactly at the cutoff is included?
Two atoms are exactly one cutoff apart. Can your floating-point distance put them just beyond it? How do you keep the boundary exact?

templates.title: Ablation pairs — runs in a sweep whose configs differ in exactly one hyperparameter
templates.subtopic: one masked signature per key, grouping instead of pairwise comparison, config normalisation

sections.scenario: Researchers launch sweeps: many runs of one experiment with different hyperparameters. To read a sweep as an ablation they compare two runs whose configs differ in exactly one hyperparameter, so that a difference in results can be traced to that one change. The experiment tracker should list every such pair for {{sweep}}, with the hyperparameter that differs, as soon as the sweep's configs are known. Runs that repeat a config exactly are reruns, not ablations, and must not be listed.
sections.problem: Implement ablation_pairs(runs, ignore=(), defaults=None). runs is a list of (run_id, config), where config is a dict from key to value. Run ids are unique strings of a fixed width. Keys in ignore are never compared. A run's effective config is its config, with any key it omits taken from defaults, and without the ignored keys. Two runs form an ablation pair on key k when their effective configs differ in k and agree on every other key. Return every pair as (run_a, run_b, k) with run_a < run_b, sorted by run_a, then run_b, then k. Runs whose effective configs are identical are never a pair. Return [] when there are no pairs. {{level_rule}}
sections.constraints: The timing check is a sweep of 24 000 runs with ten hyperparameters of four values each. Comparing every pair is 288 million comparisons. Grouping by one hyperparameter first does not save you: with four values, each group still holds about 6 000 runs. Something close to O(n·k) dictionary operations (on signatures of length k) plus the size of the output is expected.
sections.assumptions: Runs, configs and values are synthetic. Values are numbers, strings or booleans, and the values of one key always have the same type, so == is the comparison. Configs are flat: nested configs are out of scope until the follow-ups. A pair says only that two configs differ in one key; whether one run per config supports a conclusion is not this function's question.
sections.criteria: Exactly one differing key per pair, identical configs excluded; every pair among several values of one key; pairs ordered within and sorted overall; ignored keys never compared at Hard and Very Hard; defaults filled for omitted keys without treating 0.0 or False as missing at Very Hard; masked signatures (or an equivalent hashing scheme) close to O(n·k) plus output, with a clear argument for why grouping by one key stays quadratic; sensible answers on two-key pairs, value normalisation, nested configs and incremental updates.

clarifications.q: If three runs differ only in the learning rate, how many pairs is that?
clarifications.a: Three: every two of them.

clarifications.q: Two runs have exactly the same config. Are they a pair?
clarifications.a: No. They differ in no key; they are reruns.

clarifications.q: Does the order of keys in a config matter?
clarifications.a: No. A config is a dict: the same keys and values are the same config whatever the order.

clarifications.q: Which run comes first in a pair?
clarifications.a: The smaller run id as a string. Ids have a fixed width, so string order is the order you would expect.

clarifications.q: Can the same pair appear twice with different keys?
clarifications.a: No. A pair that differs in exactly one key has exactly one key to report.

hints: Two runs differ in exactly key k when they agree on every key except k, and disagree on k.

For each key k, build a signature from the run's values for every other key, in a fixed key order, and group runs by it. Inside a group, two runs with different values for k are a pair; two with the same value are identical configs.
Normalise each config once, before any signature: a fixed key order, defaults filled in, ignored keys dropped. Never fill a default with or.
followups: Researchers also want pairs that differ in at most two keys. How does the signature approach extend, and what does it cost with ten keys?

One run logged a learning rate as 3e-4 and another as a value computed in code that prints as 0.00030000000000000003. Should they match, and how would you normalise values without hiding real differences?
Configs become nested (optimizer.beta2, model.layers), with lists for some values. How would you flatten them, and what counts as one hyperparameter?
New runs join the sweep every few minutes. How would you keep the pairs up to date without recomputing them all?

rules.ask: How many pairs of runs are there at 24 000 runs, and how many key comparisons does that make?
Which key do you group by first? With four values for it, how many runs share a group, and what do you do inside the group?
How do you build the signature so the same config always gives the same key, whatever the order of keys in its dict?
A run sets dropout to 0.0 explicitly and the default is 0.1. Walk through what your lookup returns.
You compare configs as strings. What happens to key order, and to 0.1 written as 0.10?

templates.title: Debug the checkpoint retention planner
templates.subtopic: per-run keep-last, metric direction, inclusive step rules, composite keys, deterministic ties

sections.scenario: Training runs save checkpoints often, and checkpoint storage fills up. A nightly retention planner decides which checkpoints to delete under a policy: keep the most recent checkpoints of each run, the best ones by an evaluation metric, every Nth step as a sparse history of the run, and anything an evaluation still points at. Researchers have reported several problems. A team's short runs lost all their recent checkpoints on a night when another team's long run was in the same batch. For a loss metric, the planner kept the worst checkpoints as "best". The step-0 checkpoint, the starting point every ablation compares with, was deleted although the policy keeps every Nth step. A pin on one run's checkpoint kept the same step in every other run. And when two checkpoints have the same metric, the one kept as best changes from night to night. The planner below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix plan_deletions(checkpoints, policy, pins) so that it meets this specification. {{retention_rule}}

  1. Checkpoints. checkpoints are dicts {"run", "step", "metric"}, one per saved checkpoint; (run, step) is unique. The list is in no particular order.
  2. Policy. policy is {"keep_last", "keep_best", "metric_mode", "every"}: keep_last and keep_best are integers of 0 or more, metric_mode is "min" (lower is better, as for a loss) or "max" (higher is better, as for an accuracy), and every is a positive integer.
  3. What is kept. A checkpoint is kept when any of these holds: it is among the keep_last highest steps of its own run; it is among the keep_best best metrics of its own run, where ties on the metric go to the earlier step; its step is a multiple of every, step 0 included; or (run, step) is in pins.
  4. Pins. pins is a list of (run, step) pairs. A pin protects exactly that checkpoint. A pin on a checkpoint that is not in the list (already deleted) changes nothing.
  5. Output. The (run, step) pairs of every checkpoint that is not kept, sorted by run and then step.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name, arguments and output format. Up to 100 000 checkpoints and 5 000 pins, processed in close to linear time.
sections.assumptions: Runs, steps, metrics and pins are synthetic, and so is the policy; check current docs for any real tool's retention rules. The planner only produces a plan: deletion happens elsewhere, so the plan must be right before anything is removed.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom for researchers; the last keep_last checkpoints kept in each run; the metric direction taken from "min" and "max"; ties on the metric broken by the earlier step whatever the input order; step 0 kept by the every-Nth rule; pins matched on (run, step); minimal fixes that keep the output format and stay close to linear; a regression test per bug; sensible answers on in-progress checkpoints, dry runs and safe deletion.

clarifications.q: Is "most recent" by step or by the time the file was written?
clarifications.a: By step.

clarifications.q: Is step 0 a multiple of every?
clarifications.a: Yes. 0 % every == 0, so the starting checkpoint is kept by that rule.

clarifications.q: Two checkpoints of a run tie for the best metric and keep_best is 1. Which is kept?
clarifications.a: The earlier step, whatever order they arrive in.

clarifications.q: A checkpoint is kept by two rules. Does it count twice towards anything?
clarifications.a: No. The rules only decide whether it is kept; it is kept once.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The checks point at each one.

hints: Run the planner on two runs with very different step counts and keep_last = 2. Which run keeps what?
Print lower_is_better for a policy whose metric_mode is "min".
What does 0 and anything evaluate to in Python?
What identifies a checkpoint, and what does pinned_steps hold?
Python's sort is stable. When two metrics are equal, which checkpoint comes first, and why does that depend on the input?
followups: A training job is still writing a checkpoint while the planner runs. How do you make sure a half-written checkpoint is never planned for deletion, or counted as the latest?
Researchers want a dry run that says, for every kept checkpoint, which rule kept it. How would you change the output without breaking existing callers?
A pin is added after the plan is computed and before the deletion runs. How do you make deletion safe?
Checkpoints are sharded over many files, and a deletion fails halfway through one. What state do you record, and what does the next night's run do?

rules.ask: Python's sort is stable. Why does that make ties depend on the input order, and which sort key makes the result independent of it?
What identifies a checkpoint? Show a pin that protects the wrong checkpoint in the original code.
Where else in a data pipeline can a value of 0 be treated as missing, and how would a test catch it?
Which other rule in the policy is per run, and how would you test that it stays per run?
The plan is computed at 01:00 and deletion runs at 03:00. What could change in between, and what does the deletion step check first?

templates.title: Experiment tracker ingestion — runs, configs and metric points from many jobs, with resumed runs, late writes and fast comparisons
templates.subtopic: client batching, idempotent ingestion, step rewrites after resume, time-series layout and downsampling for comparisons

sections.scenario: A research lab's experiment tracker records every training and evaluation run: who launched it, its config and seed, its code version, the checkpoints it saved, and its metric points. At any moment about {{active_runs}} runs are writing, each logging {{metrics_per_step}} metrics {{log_interval}} through a client library inside the job. Jobs are pre-empted and resumed from their last checkpoint, so a resumed run writes steps it has already written. Some jobs buffer metrics when the network is slow and send them minutes or hours later. Researchers open a sweep and overlay a metric for up to {{compare_runs}} runs at once, and expect the chart and a table of final values to load in a few seconds.
sections.problem: Design the tracker's ingestion and storage. Cover the client library (buffering, batching, retries, what happens when the tracker is down), the write API and how a batch is made idempotent, how a resume is recorded and which value of a rewritten step is shown, how late points land, the storage layout for metric points and for run metadata (config, seed, code version, checkpoints), how a comparison of {{compare_runs}} runs is served in seconds, and what the tracker does when a job writes far more than expected.
sections.constraints: A training job must never slow down or fail because the tracker is slow or down. A retried batch must never create duplicate points. After a resume, the chart must show one value per step, the one from the attempt that is still running, while the overwritten values stay available for debugging. A comparison must not read every raw point of every run. Configs and seeds are written once, when the run starts, and never changed afterwards.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, intervals and limits are hypothetical, and nothing here describes how the lab's own tools are built; check current docs for any real product's behaviour. Each job knows its run id, an attempt number that grows with every resume, and the step of each point. Clocks on training hosts can disagree by seconds.
sections.criteria: A client that never blocks or fails training, with bounded buffers and an explicit policy when they fill; batch identities and upserts that make retries harmless; attempts recorded and the latest attempt's value shown per step, superseded values kept; late points landing in place; a storage layout split between immutable run metadata and time-series points; summaries and min/max-preserving downsampled series for comparisons of {{compare_runs}} runs; limits on metric names and points per run with clear feedback; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: What is a step rewrite?
clarifications.a: A job pre-empted at step 12 400 resumes from its checkpoint at step 12 000 and writes steps 12 001 to 12 400 again, with different values.

clarifications.q: Which value of a rewritten step does the chart show?
clarifications.a: The value from the latest attempt. Older values stay queryable, marked as superseded.

clarifications.q: How late can points arrive?
clarifications.a: Usually seconds; after a network problem, hours. Points for a run that has finished can still arrive.

clarifications.q: Do researchers need every raw point in the chart?
clarifications.a: No, but a spike or a divergence must stay visible after any downsampling.

clarifications.q: Can one job write a huge number of metrics by mistake?
clarifications.a: Yes. A bug can log one metric per parameter or per example; the tracker must survive it.

hints: Give every batch an identity (run, attempt, client sequence number) so that a retry is recognisable, and make writes upserts keyed by (run, attempt, metric, step).
Store points per attempt and resolve "the value at this step" by the highest attempt that wrote it, instead of deleting the older attempt's points.
For comparisons, precompute per-run summaries (final value, best value) and downsampled series that keep the minimum and maximum of each bucket, so a spike survives.
followups: The tracker is down for an hour. What does the client do with an hour of points, and how does the backlog drain without overloading the tracker when it comes back?
A job logs a new metric name for every example, and the run reaches two million metric names. Where do you stop it, and what does the researcher see?
A researcher compares {{compare_runs}} runs that each have five million steps. Walk through the query and what it reads.
Two attempts of the same run disagree at step 12 300 by a large amount. How does the tracker help someone see that the resume changed the run's behaviour?

rules.ask: Points for one run land on several partitions. How do you keep a resumed attempt's rewrite from being applied before the original points it replaces?
Attempt 1's late points for step 12 300 arrive after attempt 2 wrote the same step. Which value does the chart show, and why?
A loss spike lasts three steps out of five million. Does it survive your downsampling into 1 000 points?
Two hosts' clocks disagree by seconds. Which field orders the points, and where does the timestamp still matter?
A batch is retried after a timeout, but the first attempt was in fact stored. What makes the second one harmless?

incidents: A job resumed from step 12 000 after a pre-emption, but its buffered points from the first attempt arrived twenty minutes later and replaced the second attempt's values for steps 12 001 to 12 400 on the chart, so a learning-rate change looked as if it had done nothing.
One sweep's runs logged a metric per parameter group by mistake, the metric names table grew by millions of rows in an hour, and comparisons slowed down for every team.
The tracker's write API was down for forty minutes, client buffers filled, and some jobs dropped points silently while others stalled their training loop waiting to send.

templates.title: Structure database release pipeline — predictions aligned to a catalogue snapshot, per-organism archives with checksums, and one switch for the API and the website
templates.subtopic: snapshot alignment, validation gates, content-addressed archives and manifests, an atomic release pointer

sections.scenario: A public database of predicted protein structures publishes a new release a few times a year. Each release is aligned to one snapshot of a public sequence catalogue: an entry exists for a catalogue accession at a given sequence version, and its prediction must have been computed for exactly that sequence. A release holds about {{entries}} entries, each with a structure file, per-residue confidence values and a predicted aligned error file, and offers bulk archives for {{organisms}} organisms, each with checksums. Between two releases about {{changed_share}} of entries change: new sequences, sequences whose catalogue version changed, entries recomputed by a newer model version, and sequences withdrawn from the catalogue. When a release goes live, the website, the API and the bulk download index must move to it together, within {{switch_minutes}} minutes, and nobody may see one entry's files from two releases.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that turns a catalogue snapshot and a set of computed predictions into a published release. Cover how the snapshot is pinned and compared with the previous one to decide which entries are new, unchanged, recomputed or withdrawn; how each prediction is matched to the exact sequence it was computed for; the validation gates a release must pass before it can go live; how files are named and stored so unchanged entries are not copied; how per-organism archives and their checksums and manifests are built; how the website, the API and the download index switch to the release together; and how a bad release is rolled back.
sections.constraints: A prediction computed for an older sequence version must never be published under a newer one. Unchanged entries keep their files byte for byte and are not recomputed or re-uploaded. Every archive has a checksum that users can verify, and the manifest lists every file with its checksum. The switch to a release completes within {{switch_minutes}} minutes, and a rollback to the previous release is just as fast. Files of past releases stay available.
sections.assumptions: Entry counts, organism counts, change rates and the switch window are hypothetical; how the real database is built and published is not described here, so check current docs. The sequence catalogue publishes numbered snapshots with a sequence version per accession. Predictions are computed by a separate job and handed over with the sequence checksum they were computed for. The data is predictions only: nothing here draws a medical or clinical conclusion from them.
sections.criteria: A pinned catalogue snapshot diffed against the previous one by accession and sequence checksum; predictions matched to the exact sequence they were computed for; hard validation gates (sequence match, file integrity, completeness per organism, counts reconciled with the diff) and recorded sign-off; immutable content-addressed files with unchanged entries carried over by reference; per-organism archives with checksums and a manifest, rebuilt only when they change; one release pointer read by the website, the API and the download index, switched and rolled back within {{switch_minutes}} minutes; past releases kept; a plan for each incident.

clarifications.q: How do you know a prediction matches the catalogue's sequence?
clarifications.a: Each prediction records a checksum of the sequence it was computed for; the snapshot has the current sequence for every accession. They must be equal.

clarifications.q: What happens to an entry whose accession was withdrawn from the catalogue?
clarifications.a: It leaves the new release, its old versions stay available, and the release notes list it.

clarifications.q: Are long proteins one entry?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, long sequences are predicted as overlapping fragments, each its own entry with a fragment number.

clarifications.q: Is the serving layer part of this design?
clarifications.a: Only the switch: what you publish, and the single change that makes the website, the API and the download index use the new release. Caching and traffic are another exercise.

clarifications.q: Who decides that a release can go live?
clarifications.a: The validation gates, then a person who signs it off; record both.

hints: Diff the new catalogue snapshot against the previous one by accession and sequence checksum: the diff decides which entries need new predictions, which are carried over and which are withdrawn.
Name every file by entry, version and content hash in an immutable store; a release is then a manifest that points at files, and carried-over entries point at the files they already had.
Make "the live release" one small pointer that the website, the API and the download index all read, and change only that pointer when the release goes live.
followups: Two days before a release, the catalogue publishes a newer snapshot. Do you rebase on it? What does the diff tell you, and what does it cost?
A validation gate finds that 0.4% of predictions in one organism were computed for an older sequence version. What do you do with that organism and with the release?
A research group mirrors every per-organism archive. How do you let them download only what changed, and prove that their copy is complete?
A bug is found in a released file format after release. How do you publish a fix without changing files that people have already cited and checksummed?

rules.ask: {{changed_share}} of entries changed. How much data does your release move, and how do you avoid copying the rest?
Who computes the checksum, from which bytes, and how does a user check an archive against the manifest?
The API switched and the website did not. What does a user see in that minute, and how does your design make that impossible?
Which gates are hard failures and which only warn? Give one of each and say who can override it.
You roll back after the download index was published. What happens to someone halfway through downloading an archive of the bad release?

incidents: A release went live with predictions for a few thousand accessions whose sequence had changed in the catalogue snapshot, because the matching step compared accessions without sequence checksums.
The per-organism archives for {{organisms}} organisms were rebuilt for every release, although most entries were unchanged, and the release took days longer than planned and doubled the storage bill.

During a switch, the API moved to the new release while the website's entry pages still read the old one, and for {{switch_minutes}} minutes users saw structures that did not match the confidence values on the page.

templates.title: Experiments as data — projects, runs, layered configs, seeds, code versions, checkpoints, and a run's exact recipe as of a date
templates.subtopic: immutable content-addressed config layers, per-key provenance, effective-dated named recipes, append-only run metadata

sections.scenario: A research lab runs about {{runs_per_week}} experiment runs a week across many projects. A run's configuration is assembled from up to {{config_layers}} layers: a shared base, a project default, an experiment file, the values a sweep generated for that run, and command-line overrides, each later layer overriding keys set by earlier ones. A resolved config has up to {{config_keys}} keys. Every run also records its seeds (data order, initialisation, evaluation sampling), a code version (a commit plus a hash of any uncommitted changes), a container image, the id of the training data snapshot it read, and the checkpoints it writes, about {{checkpoints_per_run}} per run. Researchers keep named recipes, such as "the current baseline for project P", and repoint them as the work moves on. Two questions keep coming up and today neither has a reliable answer: exactly what did run X use, and what did "the baseline" mean on a given date, as recorded then?
sections.problem: Design the data model for experiments. Cover projects, experiments and runs; config layers as stored documents; each run's resolved config with the layer that set each key; seeds; code version and environment; the data snapshot reference; checkpoints with step, location, checksum and retention state; named recipes and their history; and run metadata people edit later (status, tags, notes, a run marked invalid). Show how you answer: the exact recipe of run X; the difference between two runs' resolved configs, each difference attributed to its layer; what a named recipe pointed at on date D, both as recorded on D and as corrected since; and which runs used a shared layer that was later found to contain a mistake.
sections.constraints: A run's recipe never changes after the run starts: editing a shared base later must not change any past run's resolved config. Layers and resolved configs are stored in a canonical form (sorted keys, normalised numbers and booleans) so equal configs get equal hashes. Edits to run metadata are recorded with the editor's role and the time, never overwritten. Checkpoint files can be deleted by a retention policy, but their records stay. In this exercise a run that continues with a changed config is a new run that starts from the earlier run's checkpoint, linked to it.
sections.assumptions: Run volumes, layer counts, key counts and checkpoint counts are hypothetical. Metric points a run logs, and their ingestion, are out of scope (another exercise); so are accelerator scheduling and the training loop. Nothing here describes how any lab tracks its own experiments.
sections.criteria: Immutable, content-addressed layers and a resolved config per run with per-key provenance; canonical hashing with its normalisation rules stated; seeds, code version (commit plus a hash of uncommitted changes), environment and data snapshot recorded per run; checkpoints with step, checksum and retention state; named recipes as effective-dated pointers with a recorded time; metadata edits append-only and queryable as of a date; queries for the exact recipe, attributed differences, the recipe on a date and runs affected by a bad layer; storage sized for the stated volumes; incidents explained by the model and fixed without rewriting history.

clarifications.q: Is a layer just a file in the repository?
clarifications.a: It may start as one, but the tracker stores the exact content it resolved (or a content hash pointing at stored content). The file can change afterwards.

clarifications.q: How are sweeps represented?
clarifications.a: The sweep definition is stored once; each run gets a generated layer holding its swept values.

clarifications.q: Does marking a run invalid delete it?
clarifications.a: No. It is a metadata event with a reason and a time; reports filter on the run's status as of the report's date.

clarifications.q: Who reads this model?
clarifications.a: Researchers in notebooks and a comparison page, reproducibility checks, and write-ups that cite a run by id.

clarifications.q: Can two layers set the same key?
clarifications.a: Yes, that is the point of layering; the later layer wins, and the model must say which layer won for every key.

hints: Treat every layer as an immutable, content-addressed document. A run references the ordered list of layer hashes it resolved and the hash of the resolved config.
Keep provenance per key: for each resolved key, the layer that set it last. Differences between runs then explain themselves.
A named recipe is a pointer that moves. Store its history as effective-dated rows with a recorded time, apart from the runs.
followups: Write the query for "what did the baseline of project P point at on date D, as recorded on D" and "as we know it now". When do the two differ?
A mistake is found in one key of a shared base layer. Which runs are affected, and how do you leave out runs where a later layer overrode that key?
Two runs with the same resolved config hash, code version, data snapshot and seeds give different final metrics. What else would you have wanted recorded?

At {{runs_per_week}} runs a week with up to {{config_keys}} keys each, how do you store resolved configs so that both "show run X" and "all runs in project P where the learning rate came from a sweep" are fast?

rules.ask: Someone asks for every run last month whose learning-rate schedule came from the project default rather than a sweep. Can your blob answer that, and how fast?
The shared base file was edited after 3,000 runs used it. What does your model return for those runs' configs today?
A run was marked invalid by mistake and restored a week later. Which reports changed in between, and how does your model show that?
Two configs differ only in key order and in writing 0.0003 versus 3e-4. Do they hash equal in your design, and should they?
At {{config_keys}} keys per run and {{runs_per_week}} runs a week, how many rows is that in a year, and how do you rebuild one run's full config quickly?

incidents: A write-up cites a run whose resolved config, re-rendered from its stored layers, no longer matches what the run logged: layers had been stored by file path, and the shared base file was edited after the run.

After a named recipe was repointed, a weekly report of "runs on the baseline" rewrote last month's numbers: it joined runs to the recipe's current target instead of the target in force when each run started.
With up to {{config_keys}} keys per run, a key-per-row table of resolved configs grew to billions of rows, and the comparison page timed out on sweeps with many runs.

templates.title: Training data snapshots as data — sources, licence records, filtering and deduplication passes, manifests, and which runs read which snapshot
templates.subtopic: source versions and licence records, pass runs with reconciling counts, immutable manifests, record-to-shard index, run consumption by shard

dedup_scope: exact matches across all sources in the snapshot
exact and near matches across all sources in the snapshot

sections.scenario: A research lab builds training data snapshots from about {{sources}} sources. Each source arrives in versions, and each source version carries a licence record: the terms and the uses they permit, as the lab's reviewers recorded them. A snapshot is built by a pipeline of passes: format and language filters, a quality filter with a threshold you are given, deduplication of {{dedup_scope}}, and a mix with a weight per source. The output is about {{shards_per_snapshot}} shard files with checksums, and about {{snapshots_per_month}} snapshots are built a month. Training runs read snapshots by id. The catalogue never stores the documents themselves: it holds manifests, counts and checksums. It must answer: which runs read data from source S version V; what each pass removed, in counts; and, when a licence record is corrected or a source's owner withdraws some records, which snapshots and runs are affected and what the replacement snapshot contains.
sections.problem: Design the data model for training data snapshots. Cover sources and source versions; licence records and their history; pass definitions with versions and parameters; a snapshot build as an ordered list of pass runs, with records in and out per source; deduplication outcomes in counts, including pairs whose copies come from two sources; the manifest of shards with checksums and per-source counts; snapshot status (building, ready, superseded, withdrawn) with reasons; and the link from training runs, and their checkpoints, to the snapshots and shards they read. Show the queries for: the per-source funnel of one snapshot; every run that read any record of source S version V; and the snapshots, runs and checkpoints affected by a withdrawal.
sections.constraints: No document contents, text, excerpts or samples are stored in the catalogue; records are identified by opaque ids assigned at ingestion. A snapshot is immutable once ready: a fix is a new snapshot that supersedes it. Counts must reconcile: per source, records in = records removed by each pass + records out. Licence records belong to the reviewers; the pipeline reads them and never edits them. In this exercise, when copies of one record come from several sources, deduplication keeps the copy from the source with the lowest priority number (this exercise's rule).
sections.assumptions: Source counts, shard counts, build frequency and the priority rule are hypothetical. Interpreting a licence is a reviewer's decision recorded as data; the model never decides it. Nothing here describes any lab's actual data, sources or licences.
sections.criteria: Sources, versions and licence records kept apart, with licence history and the record each build read; pass runs with parameters and per-source counts that reconcile, checked; cross-source deduplication outcomes recorded in counts with the stated keep rule; immutable manifests with checksums and a superseding relation; a record-to-shard index for withdrawals with no content; run consumption at shard grain; withdrawal impact queries over snapshots, runs and checkpoints; incremental replacement builds that recompute deduplication correctly; sizes estimated; incidents explained by the model.

clarifications.q: Does a run read a whole snapshot?
clarifications.a: Not always. It reads shards in an order and may stop or switch mix part-way. Record which shards it actually read.

clarifications.q: Can a withdrawal cover only part of a source version?
clarifications.a: Yes. A withdrawal names a source version and either all of it or a list of record ids.

clarifications.q: Are pass parameters part of a snapshot's identity?
clarifications.a: Yes. Two builds from the same inputs with a different quality threshold are different snapshots.

clarifications.q: Do we need lineage for every record?
clarifications.a: Only enough to answer "which shards of which snapshots hold record R": an index from record id to shard, built with the manifest, never the content.

clarifications.q: Does a licence correction change past snapshots?
clarifications.a: The snapshots do not change; the model must show which licence record each build read and which record is in force now.

hints: Separate definitions (sources, versions, licence records, pass definitions) from builds (snapshots, pass runs with counts) and from consumption (runs reading shards).
Store counts in and out per pass and per source. The funnel and the reconciliation check both come from those rows.
A deduplication pass across sources needs one more count per pair of sources: records kept from one source whose duplicates in another were removed. That is what a withdrawal disturbs.
followups: Write the reconciliation check for one snapshot. What do you do with a snapshot that fails it?
Source S withdraws 2% of its records. Which snapshots, runs and checkpoints are affected, and how do you build the replacement without rerunning every pass on every source?

With deduplication of {{dedup_scope}}, the withdrawn records had been the kept copies of many duplicate pairs. What happens to the other copies in the replacement snapshot, and how do the counts show it?
At {{snapshots_per_month}} snapshots a month with {{shards_per_snapshot}} shards each, how large is the record-to-shard index, and how long would you keep it?

rules.ask: The catalogue keeps no contents. How do you answer "which shards hold record R" and "how many records of source S survived deduplication" without them?
A reviewer corrects a source version's licence record six months later. Which builds read the old record, and how does your model show what was believed when each snapshot was built?
A duplicate pair spans two sources and the kept copy's source is later withdrawn. Which copy should the replacement snapshot keep, and what in your model records that?
A run read 40% of one snapshot and then switched to another mix. What does your link record, and how do you find the runs that read a withdrawn record?
A snapshot is ready and five runs have read it. One shard turns out to be corrupt. What changes in your tables, and what stays?

incidents: A withdrawal for one source version was matched against snapshots by source name only: runs that read an older, unaffected version were flagged, and a snapshot built from the affected version under a renamed source was missed.
A snapshot's per-source counts failed reconciliation by 0.4%: a filter pass was retried after a crash and its counts were recorded twice.

With deduplication of {{dedup_scope}}, a replacement snapshot built after a withdrawal had fewer records from other sources than expected: the rebuild reused the old deduplication decisions, so copies removed as duplicates of the withdrawn records stayed removed.

templates.title: Predicted structures as data — entries by catalogue accession and sequence version, model versions, fragments, per-residue confidence, aligned-error files and releases
templates.subtopic: external identity versus entry versions, fragment residue ranges, per-residue arrays versus rows, files with checksums, release membership and carry-over

fragment_rule: longer than 2,700 residues are predicted as fragments of 1,400 residues, a new fragment starting every 200 residues
longer than 2,000 residues are predicted as fragments of 1,000 residues, a new fragment starting every 500 residues

sections.scenario: A public database publishes predicted protein structures: in this exercise, one entry per sequence of a public sequence catalogue, about {{entries}} entries, with {{releases_per_year}} releases a year, each aligned to a snapshot of the catalogue. Each entry has a coordinates file, a per-residue confidence score from 0 to 100, and a predicted aligned error file: one value per pair of residues, so it grows with the square of the length (the median length is about {{median_length}} residues). In this exercise sequences {{fragment_rule}} (this exercise's rule; check current docs). Each entry is produced by a model version; a later release may recompute some entries, with a newer model version or because the catalogue changed a sequence, and carry the rest over unchanged. Researchers cite an entry by id and version, download single files, call an API, and download per-organism archives.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover catalogue accessions and sequence versions, with organism; entries and entry versions (accession, sequence version, fragment, model version); fragments and their residue ranges; per-residue confidence; summary statistics per entry version (mean confidence, and the share of residues in each of this exercise's confidence bands); aligned-error files and the other files, with format, size, checksum and storage location; releases with their catalogue snapshot, the entry versions they contain and which of those were carried over; and per-organism archives. Show how you answer: which entry version a citation "entry E, version v" refers to; which entries in release R were computed for a sequence the catalogue has since changed; the confidence of residue i of accession A in release R when A is fragmented; and every file and archive a release contains.
sections.constraints: An entry version is immutable once released; a recomputation is a new version. Residue numbers follow the catalogue sequence version, and every fragment's residue range maps onto it. Per-residue values must be retrievable for every released version; aligned-error matrices are stored as files, not as rows. In this exercise, for a residue covered by two overlapping fragments, the value comes from the fragment in which the residue is furthest from either end, ties going to the lower fragment number (this exercise's rule). The database stores predictions and their stated confidence; it draws no biological, medical or clinical conclusion from them.
sections.assumptions: Entry counts, release cadence, the fragment rule, lengths and confidence bands are hypothetical (check current docs). Serving the website, files and API under load is out of scope (another exercise). Nothing here describes how any real database stores its data.
sections.criteria: Catalogue identity, entry versions and release membership kept apart; fragments with residue ranges mapped to the catalogue numbering and the overlap rule answerable; per-residue confidence stored compactly with summary statistics for filtering; aligned-error and other files as rows with checksums and locations, not matrices in tables; immutable, citable entry versions with model versions; releases as sets with carry-over by reference and archives built from membership; sizes estimated for the stated volume; no biological or medical claims drawn from predictions; incidents explained by the model.

clarifications.q: Is one accession always one entry?
clarifications.a: One per accession and sequence version, unless the sequence is fragmented; then one entry per fragment, all tied to that accession and sequence version.

clarifications.q: When the catalogue changes a sequence, is the old entry deleted?
clarifications.a: Not from released history. A later release recomputes it or leaves it out; the old version stays citable.

clarifications.q: How big is per-residue data?
clarifications.a: One small number per residue. The aligned-error data is length squared per entry, which is why it lives in files.

clarifications.q: Are model versions compared anywhere?
clarifications.a: Not in this model. It records which model version produced each entry version; comparisons are someone else's analysis.

clarifications.q: What is in a per-organism archive?
clarifications.a: The files of exactly the entry versions that belong to that release and organism, with a checksum per archive.

hints: Separate the catalogue's identity (accession, sequence version) from the database's (entry, entry version) and from release membership.
Store per-residue confidence compactly per entry version (an array column or a columnar file) and keep summary statistics as columns for filtering.
A release is a set of entry versions plus a catalogue snapshot. Carry-over is membership, not a copy.
followups: Write the query for residue i of accession A in release R when A is fragmented under this exercise's rule.
A release recomputes 10% of the entries with a new model version and carries the rest. What rows are written, and what does each per-organism archive for that release contain?
The catalogue merges two accessions into one. What happens to their entries, to existing citations and to the next release?
At {{entries}} entries with a median length of {{median_length}}, estimate the bytes of per-residue confidence and of aligned-error files per release, and say where each lives.

rules.ask: At {{entries}} entries of about {{median_length}} residues, how many rows is that per release, and which query actually needs residue-level rows?
A paper cites entry E as it was two releases ago. Where is that version in your model, and how is it served?
The catalogue changes A's sequence and the residue numbering shifts. How does your key tell the old prediction from the new one?
Under this exercise's rule, a residue lies in two fragments. Which value does your model return, and where is that rule recorded?
An archive for one organism in one release must never change after publication. What do you store about it, and how do users verify what they downloaded?

incidents: After a release recomputed some entries with a newer model version, a per-organism archive turned out to mix entry versions from two releases: the archive builder took the latest version of each entry instead of the release's members.
Residue numbers in a fragmented entry's confidence file did not match the catalogue's numbering: fragment-local positions had been stored without the fragment's start offset.
Summary statistics for {{entries}} entries were recomputed from per-residue values in every release, carried-over entries included, and the release missed its date.

templates.title: Watermark detection results as data — detector versions, checked files by content type, segment-level results, confidence levels, and aggregates with no content kept
templates.subtopic: versioned outcome definitions, content-free file descriptors, segment results and a derived file outcome, keyed hashes with a window, suppressed aggregates

sections.scenario: A detection service checks whether content carries an imperceptible watermark of the kind SynthID's public documentation describes. It accepts {{content_types}} and runs about {{checks_per_day}} checks a day. Each check returns an outcome for the whole file and, for long or composite content, for segments: time ranges in audio and video, spans in text, regions in images. In this exercise a segment's outcome is detected, not detected or uncertain, each with a confidence level of high, medium or low, and a file's outcome is all, part or none of it watermarked, or inconclusive (this exercise's outcomes; check current docs). During a rollout up to {{live_detector_versions}} detector versions run at once. Content is never kept: a check keeps only the metadata reporting needs. Product and policy teams read reports of outcomes by content type, detector version, confidence level and day, and no cell with fewer than {{min_cell}} checks is ever shown.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover detector versions per content type, with their outcome definitions and confidence thresholds; checks (channel, requester category, time) with no identities in analytics; checked files described only by content type, format and a size or duration bucket; segment-level results; the file-level outcome derived by a stated rule, with the rule's version; repeated checks of the same file; and aggregate tables with small cells suppressed. Show how you answer: outcomes by content type, detector version and confidence level per day; the share of files with part of the content watermarked; and how results compare when the same files are checked by two detector versions during a rollout.
sections.constraints: No content, thumbnail, transcript, excerpt or anything from which content could be rebuilt is stored. To recognise repeated checks of one file, a keyed hash of the file may be kept for a limited window (this exercise's rule) and never reaches analytics. Requesters appear in analytics only as a category. Cells below {{min_cell}} checks are suppressed, including cells that could be recovered by subtracting published cells from a published total. The model records outcomes and confidence levels only: how detection works, and anything about changing or removing watermarks, is out of scope.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, content types, outcome names, confidence levels, thresholds and the hash window are hypothetical. Nothing here describes how any watermarking system or detector works internally.
sections.criteria: Detector versions and outcome rules as versioned reference data; checks, content-free file descriptors, segment results and a derived file outcome kept apart, with the rule version recorded; uncertain and inconclusive kept as outcomes of their own; repeated checks handled with a keyed hash in a limited window that never reaches analytics; requesters only as categories; aggregates per day, content type, version, outcome and confidence level with suppression applied last, complementary cells included; version-aware comparisons during rollouts; retention and sizes for the stated volume; nothing about how detection works or how a watermark could be changed; incidents explained by the model.

clarifications.q: Is an uncertain segment counted as watermarked?
clarifications.a: No. It is its own outcome and is shown apart.

clarifications.q: What makes a file "part"?
clarifications.a: In this exercise: at least one segment detected and at least one not detected. Record the rule version that produced each file-level outcome.

clarifications.q: The same file is checked three times in a day. What counts?
clarifications.a: Keep every check. Reports count checks, and count files once by their latest check in the window.

clarifications.q: Do detector versions share confidence thresholds?
clarifications.a: No. Each version has its own definitions, which is why comparing versions needs care.

clarifications.q: Can a result be corrected?
clarifications.a: If a detector version is withdrawn, its results stay, marked with the withdrawal, and reports decide whether to include them.

hints: Separate the check (request metadata), the file descriptor (no content), segment results, and the derived file-level outcome with its rule version.
Detector versions and outcome rules are reference data with effective dates; every result row names one of each.
Build aggregates from the detail into cells keyed by day, content type, detector version, outcome and confidence level, and suppress small cells as the last step, complementary cells included.
followups: Write the derivation of the file-level outcome from segment results under this exercise's rule. Where does an uncertain segment fit?
