During a rollout the same files are checked by two versions. How do you pair the results so that agreement can be measured without keeping the files?
A cell with fewer than {{min_cell}} checks is suppressed, but the row total and the other cells are published. How could someone recover it, and how does your aggregate step prevent that?
At {{checks_per_day}} checks a day, with segment results for long content, which tables hold detail and for how long, and which aggregates are kept indefinitely?

rules.ask: The rule is that no content is kept. How do you investigate a reported wrong result without it, and what could you ask the reporter for instead?
A plain hash of a public image lets anyone holding the image find its check. What do you key it with, how long do you keep it, and does analytics ever see it?
Analytics carry only a requester category. Which grain do your reports use, and where does the identifier stop?
A suppressed cell can be recovered as the row total minus the other cells. How does your aggregate step prevent that?
Each detector version defines its own confidence levels. Do you store a raw score at all, and can two versions' scores be compared?

incidents: When a new detector version reached half of the traffic, the daily share of images "part watermarked" rose sharply: the new version reported segments that the old file-level rule did not expect, and the report mixed both versions in one series.
A weekly report published a cell below {{min_cell}} checks: suppression ran before a batch of late results was merged, and the merge split one cell into two smaller ones.
Segment results for long audio made the detail table grow ten times faster than checks, and the daily aggregate job read every segment row since the start of the month.

templates.title: Predictions behind the catalogue — published structures whose sequence changed after their snapshot, and days out of date, per release and organism
templates.subtopic: as-of joins on catalogue versions, carried-over rows resolved to the computing release, entry versus sequence versions, report-date cut-offs

sections.scenario: A public database of predicted protein structures publishes a release every few months. In this exercise each release is aligned to a snapshot of a public sequence catalogue: a prediction was computed for the sequence its accession had in the catalogue on the catalogue_snapshot date of the release that computed it, and the release went public later, on released_on. The catalogue keeps changing. An accession gets a new entry_version whenever its catalogue entry is updated, and its sequence_version goes up only when the sequence itself changes (this exercise's rule; check current docs for how a real catalogue versions its entries). {{carry_rule}} The curation team wants to know, per release and organism, how many published predictions are now behind the catalogue, and for how long. The report runs as of {{as_of}}.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns release_id, organism, accessions, behind, behind_pct, avg_days_behind, max_days_behind, one row per release and organism with predictions in that release, ordered by release_id, organism.

  • The sequence version a prediction was computed for is the sequence_version of its accession's latest entry_versions row with effective_on on or before the catalogue_snapshot of the release named in predicted_in (an as-of join; a row effective on the snapshot date itself is included).
  • A prediction is behind when its accession has a row with a higher sequence_version and effective_on on or before {{as_of}}. Rows effective after {{as_of}} are ignored, so the report can be reproduced. It became behind on the earliest such effective_on, and its days behind are {{as_of}} minus that date (0 when the change is effective on {{as_of}}). A new entry version whose sequence_version did not rise is not a change.
  • {{fragment_rule}}
  • accessions is the number of distinct accessions; behind how many of them are behind; behind_pct is 100 × behind ÷ accessions, rounded to 1 decimal; avg_days_behind is the mean of their days behind, rounded to 1 decimal, and max_days_behind the largest; both are NULL when nothing is behind.
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Dates are stored as DATE; DATE - DATE is a whole number of days in PostgreSQL. Use ROUND(numeric, n). The sample has {{release_count}} releases, {{prediction_rows}} prediction rows and {{catalogue_rows}} catalogue rows; a production database of this kind holds hundreds of millions of predictions, and the catalogue's history is far larger.
sections.assumptions: Accessions (SYN…), organisms, releases, versions and dates are synthetic and do not refer to real entries. "Behind" is a data-freshness measure only: it says nothing about whether a predicted structure is right or wrong, and nothing biological or medical.
sections.criteria: The computing release resolved through predicted_in and its snapshot used for the as-of join, inclusive of the snapshot date; changes detected by sequence_version, not entry_version; the report date as an inclusive cut-off; days counted from the first change; accessions counted once, fragments included; every release and organism shown, with NULL days when nothing is behind; numeric rounding; deterministic order; can discuss back-dated catalogue rows, indexing the as-of lookup at scale, and driving the next release's recompute set from the same logic.

clarifications.q: A catalogue row is effective on the snapshot date itself. Was the prediction computed for it?
clarifications.a: Yes. The as-of join includes rows on or before catalogue_snapshot.

clarifications.q: The sequence changed after the snapshot but before the release went public. Is that prediction behind?
clarifications.a: Yes. It was already out of date on release day; its days are counted from the change.

clarifications.q: What is predicted_in?
clarifications.a: The release whose run computed the prediction. When it names an earlier release, the prediction was carried over unchanged and was computed for that release's snapshot.

clarifications.q: What if the sequence changed twice after the snapshot?
clarifications.a: The prediction is counted once, and its days run from the first change.

clarifications.q: Should a release and organism with nothing behind still appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with behind 0, behind_pct 0.0 and NULL days.

hints: Resolve the computing snapshot first: join predictions to releases on predicted_in, not on release_id, and reduce to one row per release and accession.
The as-of lookup is "the latest row on or before a date": a LATERAL subquery with ORDER BY effective_on DESC LIMIT 1, or DISTINCT ON.
A LEFT JOIN to later rows with a higher sequence_version, up to {{as_of}}, with MIN(effective_on), leaves NULL for predictions that are current; COUNT(column) then counts only the ones behind.
followups: Add a column for how many predictions were already behind on the day their release went public. Which date replaces {{as_of}}?
The catalogue sometimes back-dates a row: it is recorded today with an effective_on last month. How would you make last month's report reproducible, and what extra column does that need?

At production scale, the as-of lookup runs over hundreds of millions of predictions. Which index or pre-computed table would you build, and how would you keep it current as the catalogue changes daily?
The next release should recompute exactly the predictions that are behind. Write the anti-join that lists them, and say how you would prove afterwards that none was missed.

rules.ask: Which date fixes the sequence a prediction was computed for, and what does your query say about a sequence that changed between the snapshot and the public release?
An annotation-only update raises entry_version without touching the sequence. Does your query call that prediction behind?
Your comparison uses the catalogue's latest row. What does it do with a row dated after the report date, and could you reproduce last month's report?
Which release and organism rows disappear when nothing in them is behind, and is that what the curation team wants to see?
If a long sequence were listed as three fragment rows, what would your COUNT(*) count: accessions or rows?
How does this as-of lookup behave on hundreds of millions of predictions, and what index turns it into a seek?

incidents: After a catalogue import, the share of predictions behind jumped from a few percent to about a third overnight: the import had copied the entry version into sequence_version, so every annotation update looked like a sequence change.

A researcher reported that residue numbers in a carried-over prediction did not match the catalogue's current sequence, while this report said it was current: the report had checked carried-over predictions against the snapshot of the release that listed them, not the one that computed them.
Rerunning last quarter's report gave different numbers each time: it compared each prediction with the catalogue's latest row instead of the rows effective on or before the report date.

templates.title: Reproducing any past run — pinned code, data snapshots, seeds and environments, and an honest report of what could not be pinned
templates.subtopic: recipe capture at launch, content-addressed pinning, re-run comparison, honest reporting

sections.scenario: A research lab's {{teams}} research teams launch about {{runs_per_week}} training and evaluation runs a week, from short sweeps to runs that last weeks. A run reads a registered training data snapshot, runs code from a repository commit (often with uncommitted local changes), inside a container image, with a configuration assembled from defaults, files and command-line overrides, several random seeds, and a particular accelerator type and count. Researchers, internal reviewers before a paper is submitted, and the lab's own release reviews regularly ask the same question about a run from up to {{lookback}} ago: if we ran it again, would we get the same result?
sections.problem: Design the reproduction system. Cover what is captured when a run launches (the recipe) and how each input is pinned and retained; what cannot be pinned (an external download, a non-deterministic kernel, a retired accelerator type) and how that is recorded; the re-run service that rebuilds the environment, fetches the snapshot and launches with the same seeds; how a re-run is compared with the original (curves and final metrics, against this exercise's tolerance); the reproduction report and its outcome levels; how much it costs to keep everything reproducible for {{lookback}}; and how a reviewer can trust that the recipe and results were not changed after the fact.
sections.constraints: Capturing the recipe adds at most a few seconds to a launch, and a capture failure never silently produces a run that looks fully pinned. Re-runs never alter the original run's records. Re-runs draw on a limited accelerator budget, so the largest runs cannot simply be repeated in full. Data snapshots are far too large to copy per run. A run counts as reproduced when its final metrics fall within {{tolerance}} (relative) of the original's, by this exercise's rule.
sections.assumptions: Run counts, sizes, budgets and the tolerance are hypothetical. Training data snapshots are already registered as immutable manifests of content-addressed shards (you may rely on that). Every run and metric is synthetic; nothing here describes how any lab tracks its experiments.
sections.criteria: A recipe manifest of content hashes captured at launch, including uncommitted diffs, the fully resolved configuration, all seeds and the hardware; pinning by reference to immutable, content-addressed storage, with retention tied to the recipes that must stay reproducible for {{lookback}}; an explicit record of what could not be pinned; a re-run service that never alters the original and compares curves and final metrics against the stated tolerance; outcome levels that distinguish bitwise, within tolerance, partial, different hardware, and not reproduced (with the reason); a tamper-evident record for reviewers; cost of retention and re-runs stated; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Must a re-run be bitwise identical?
clarifications.a: No. Bitwise identity is reported when it happens, but some accelerator kernels are non-deterministic; the bar is {{tolerance}} on final metrics, by this exercise's rule.

clarifications.q: Can researchers launch from uncommitted code?
clarifications.a: Today they can. You decide whether that continues and, if so, what is captured.

clarifications.q: Can a re-run use different hardware?
clarifications.a: Sometimes the original accelerator type has been retired. The report must say when a re-run used different hardware.

clarifications.q: Are full re-runs of the largest runs affordable?
clarifications.a: No. You may propose partial reproduction (for example the first stretch of steps, or resuming from a recorded checkpoint), stated plainly as partial.

clarifications.q: Who reads the report?
clarifications.a: The researcher, internal reviewers, and occasionally outside reviewers of a paper through the researcher.

hints: Treat the recipe as a manifest of content hashes: the code tree (including any uncommitted diff), the image digest, the resolved dependency lockfile, the data snapshot id, the fully resolved configuration, every seed, the hardware topology and the launch command.
Pin by reference to immutable, content-addressed storage, and retain whatever a kept recipe references for as long as you promise to keep it.
Separate "could not be pinned" (known before any re-run) from "pinned, but the re-run differs" (found by comparing), and report both.
followups: Walk through exactly what is captured when a researcher launches a run with uncommitted changes and three configuration overrides on the command line.

A re-run's loss curve tracks the original for 10,000 steps, then drifts, and the final metric lands outside {{tolerance}}. How does the system help decide whether this is non-determinism or a changed input?
The original accelerator type has been retired. What does reproduction mean now, and how is it reported?
Storage for pinned images, snapshots and checkpoints grows faster than the budget. What do you keep for {{lookback}}, what do you let go, and how does the report reflect it?
A paper cites a run. A reviewer asks for evidence that the recorded recipe and results are the ones recorded at the time. What do you show them?

rules.ask: The image was built from a base tagged "latest" and a package index that has since changed. What exactly did you pin, and can you rebuild that image bitwise today?
The researcher ran with uncommitted local changes. What does the commit hash tell a reviewer, and what else do you capture?
Every seed is pinned and the re-run still differs. Name two sources of variation that seeds do not control, and how you would record them.
Forcing deterministic kernels slows training by a third. Do you make it the default, and for which runs?
You reproduce from a checkpoint halfway through the run. What have you shown, and what have you not shown?

incidents: A reviewer asks to reproduce a run from almost {{lookback}} ago. The container image's base layers were deleted by a registry clean-up policy, and 3% of the shards in its data snapshot were garbage-collected because only the manifest was marked as kept.

Re-runs of one recipe on the same accelerator type give final metrics that differ by up to twice {{tolerance}}. The cause turns out to be the data loader's shuffle depending on the number of loader workers, which the recipe never recorded.

A configuration library upgrade changed a default value. Runs whose recipe stored only the command-line overrides now resolve to a different configuration when re-run, and nobody notices until a reproduction fails.

templates.title: Serving a public structure database — entry pages, downloads, an API and bulk archives under heavy read load, with old releases still citable
templates.subtopic: versioned immutable objects, CDN caching, release switches, bulk delivery, citation

sections.scenario: A public database of predicted protein structures holds {{entries}} entries. Each entry is keyed by the accession of a protein in a public sequence catalogue, a fragment number (long proteins are predicted in overlapping fragments) and a model version, and has a structure file in two common formats, a per-residue confidence score for every residue, and a predicted aligned error file. People use it through entry pages on a website, direct file downloads, a REST API and bulk archives per organism and per release ({{archive_tb}} TB per release). Traffic peaks at about {{peak_rps}} requests a second, with sudden spikes when a widely read paper links to entries, and steady load from automated pipelines that download in bulk. A new release appears a few times a year and replaces many entries; the {{past_releases}} previous releases must stay downloadable, and a paper that cites an entry at a version must always resolve to exactly the files it used.
sections.problem: Design the serving system. Cover the storage layout and object naming; how "latest" is served alongside version-pinned addresses; caching at the edge and in front of the origin, and the cache keys; how a release switch keeps every page, file and API response for an entry on one version; the API (lookup by accession, by entry id and version, and batched lookups) and how it is protected from abusive clients without a login; bulk archive delivery (mirrors, a cloud bucket, checksums, resumable downloads); stable identifiers for citation; monitoring of what users actually receive; and the cost of egress.
sections.constraints: A user must never see an entry with files from two different releases (for example a new structure coloured by old confidence values). The latest alias switches for every entry within one hour of a release being declared live. A version-pinned address never changes content, ever. Downloads are public, with no login. Origin capacity is a fraction of peak traffic, so most reads must be served from caches. Egress cost is a stated budget.
sections.assumptions: Entry counts, traffic, archive sizes, the release cadence and the identifier scheme are hypothetical and this exercise's rule (check current docs). Releases are built and checked by a separate pipeline that hands you a complete, immutable set of files with a manifest. The data is predictions only: nothing here draws a medical or clinical conclusion from them.
sections.criteria: Immutable, version-named objects with "latest" as a small pointer; long-lived caching of immutable files and short, bounded caching of pointers, with normalised cache keys; a page, its files and its API response resolved from one version so they never mix; a release switch that changes pointers only and completes within the hour; old releases served correctly at lower cost tiers; bulk delivery through manifests with checksums, stable names and incremental sync; protection from heavy clients keyed on something other than logins, with fair treatment of shared addresses; stable versioned identifiers for citation, including withdrawn entries; monitoring of what users actually receive; egress cost addressed; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do entry ids carry the version?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, an entry id is accession, fragment and model version; the website also offers an address without the version that means "latest".

clarifications.q: Are old releases served as fast as the latest?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily. They must stay correct and downloadable; you decide how much performance they get.

clarifications.q: Who are the bulk users?
clarifications.a: Research groups and other databases that mirror whole organisms or whole releases, often on a schedule.

clarifications.q: Is there a search box?
clarifications.a: By accession, protein name and organism; free-text search over annotations is out of scope.

clarifications.q: Can an entry disappear in a release?
clarifications.a: Yes, when its sequence is withdrawn from the catalogue. Its old versions stay citable; the latest address says it was withdrawn and when.

hints: Make every file immutable and name it by version (or by content hash). "Latest" is then a small, separately cached pointer, and a release switch changes only pointers.
Cache the immutable objects for a very long time and the pointers for a short, bounded time; render pages from one resolved version so a page and its files cannot disagree.
Bulk users need manifests with checksums and stable archive names more than they need speed; most of them would rather sync a difference than re-download everything.
followups: Walk through a request for an entry's page during the minute a new release goes live. Which version does the user see, and how do you guarantee the page and its files agree?
A paper's link goes viral and a few thousand entries receive ten times normal traffic. What absorbs it, and what reaches the origin?
A research group mirrors every release. How do you let them fetch only what changed, and verify it?
A small number of clients send millions of API calls a day, crowding out everyone else. How do you protect the service without requiring logins?
An error is found in one release after it went live. How do you correct it while keeping citations to the original files resolvable and honest?

rules.ask: What is the cache key for an entry's confidence file, and what happens to a cached copy when the latest version changes?
Your pages and your files have different lifetimes in the cache. Describe the minute in which a user can see a new structure with old confidence values, and how you close it.
Downloads are public with no login. What do you key the limit on, and what happens to a whole university behind one address?
A paper cites an entry's version from {{past_releases}} releases ago. What does the link resolve to, and what does the page say about newer versions?
A mirror's checksum check fails on one archive. How does the mirror know whether the file or the checksum list is wrong?

incidents: A widely read article links to a few thousand entries using addresses with tracking query strings. Every variant misses the edge cache, origin load reaches four times its capacity, and entry pages time out while traffic is still below {{peak_rps}} requests a second.

For forty minutes after a release switch, some users see new structure files on pages that still colour residues by the previous release's confidence values, because the page and the confidence file were cached under different lifetimes.

One automated client re-downloads the full {{archive_tb}} TB release archive every day, because the archive's last-modified time changed when the files were re-uploaded to a new bucket, and egress for the month passes its budget in eleven days.

templates.title: Watermark detection reporting — outcomes across images, video, audio and text, detector rollouts, and measured disagreement between versions
templates.subtopic: outcome records without content, aggregation thresholds, version rollouts, shadow comparison

sections.scenario: A research lab's generative tools embed an imperceptible watermark in the images, video, audio and text they produce, and the lab offers a detector: partners and users submit a file, and the detector reports whether all of it, part of it, or none of it appears to carry the watermark, with a confidence level (for video and audio, which time ranges; this exercise's outcome categories, check current docs). About {{checks_per_day}} checks arrive a day through a web tool and partner integrations. New detector versions are rolled out gradually, starting with {{rollout_share}} of traffic. Policy and product teams want weekly aggregate outcomes per content type, channel and confidence level, and the people deciding on a rollout want to know how often the new version disagrees with the old one, and in which direction.
sections.problem: Design the detection reporting system. Cover the outcome record each check produces (and everything it must not contain); how checked content is discarded; how repeated checks of the same file are recognised without keeping the file; the aggregation pipeline and its publication rules (cells below {{min_cell}} checks are never shown, by this exercise's rule); how traffic is assigned to detector versions during a rollout; how disagreement between versions is measured when production content cannot be kept for replay; how a version change and a change in the mix of submitted content are told apart in the reports; and retention of outcome records for {{record_days}} days.
sections.constraints: No checked content is kept, and nothing is stored from which content could be reconstructed. Every published number is an aggregate over at least {{min_cell}} checks, and no breakdown may let a reader isolate a single partner's or user's activity. A check's response time must not grow by more than a small, stated margin because of reporting. Reports must say which detector versions they cover. This system is about measuring and reporting detection outcomes only: it does not cover how watermarks are embedded, and it never covers ways to remove, weaken or evade one.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, rollout shares, thresholds and retention are hypothetical and this exercise's rule (check current docs). The detector itself is a service you call; you do not design it. The lab keeps a separate test set of files it generated itself for testing, under its own policy, which may be replayed through any detector version.
sections.criteria: An outcome record with deliberately chosen fields and no content, written at the end of the check, with content discarded in the same request and all logging paths tested; repeated checks recognised by a keyed, rotated hash within the stated retention; aggregates with a minimum cell size applied at publication time to every published breakdown, and protection against recovering small cells by subtraction; version assignment by a stable hash independent of content type and partner, with mix checks between cohorts; disagreement measured by dual-running a sample of live checks and recording only paired outcomes, plus replays on the lab's own test set; reports that state version coverage and separate mix shift from detector change; no removal or evasion detail anywhere; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: May we keep a hash of each file to count repeated checks?
clarifications.a: By this exercise's rule, a keyed hash with a key rotated every {{record_days}} days may be kept with the outcome record; nothing else derived from the content.

clarifications.q: What is in an outcome record?
clarifications.a: Time, channel, content type, coarse size and duration buckets, detector version, the outcome, the confidence level and, for video and audio, how many segments were flagged. You decide whether anything else is justified.

clarifications.q: Can we replay last week's production traffic through a new version?
clarifications.a: No; it was never kept. Replays are possible only on the lab's own test set.

clarifications.q: Who reads the aggregates?
clarifications.a: Internal policy and product teams weekly, and partners see aggregates of their own channel.

clarifications.q: How long does a rollout take?
clarifications.a: Several weeks, from {{rollout_share}} of traffic to all of it, with a decision at each step.

hints: Write the outcome record at the end of the check, from fields chosen on purpose; drop the content in the same request, and test that no log, trace or error path keeps it.
Since production content cannot be replayed, measure disagreement while the content is still in hand: run both versions on a sampled share of live checks and record only the pair of outcomes.
Assign versions by a stable hash of something that does not correlate with content type or partner, and compare cohorts with the same mix, or the comparison measures traffic rather than the detector.
followups: Walk through one video check from upload to the weekly report. What exists, where, and for how long?
How do you measure how often the new version disagrees with the old one, by content type and confidence level, without keeping any content?
The weekly share of "not detected" for audio rises after a rollout step. How do you tell a version regression from a change in what was submitted?

A partner asks for a per-day breakdown of their channel by content type and confidence level. Which cells can you show, and how do you stop a reader from subtracting one published total from another to recover a small cell?
A rollout reviewer asks for a single number that says the new version is "better". What do you give them instead, and why?

rules.ask: The rule says no checked content is kept. How do you debug a surprising outcome without it?
Could your hash let someone confirm that a particular file was checked? What key, rotation and retention make that acceptable here?
Running both versions doubles the cost of a check. What share do you sample, and how many disagreements do you need before a difference in one content type means something?
What do you hash on to assign a check to a version, and how do you prove that both cohorts received the same mix of content types and channels?
Two published totals differ by one small cell. How does your publication rule prevent that subtraction?

incidents: After the new version reaches {{rollout_share}} of traffic, the weekly report shows the share of audio checks with "not detected" up six points in its cohort. Version assignment had been by partner, and the partner placed in the new cohort mostly submits older recordings made before any watermarking existed.

A partner-level weekly breakdown published a cell of four checks, below the {{min_cell}} threshold, because the threshold was applied before the data was split again by confidence level for a new chart.

A partner integration's retry bug submits each file up to five times. That partner's channel shows checks up fourfold and its outcome shares shift, because repeated checks of the same file were counted as separate checks in the weekly aggregates.

templates.title: Research compute allocation — proposals, quarterly allocations by a stated rule, usage against allocation, and mid-quarter reallocation
templates.subtopic: reproducible allocation runs, grants ledger, burn tracking, reallocation with explanations

sections.scenario: A research organisation shares a pool of about {{pool}} accelerator-hours a quarter (synthetic) among its projects. Before each quarter, projects submit proposals, {{proposals}} of them: the accelerator-hours they need per month and per accelerator type, the milestones the hours buy, and a justification. A review panel scores the proposals, and allocations follow a published rule: proposals are placed in funding tiers by score, higher tiers receive their request (possibly trimmed), lower tiers share what remains in proportion to their requests, and {{reserve}} of the pool is held back for urgent requests during the quarter. Usage comes from the cluster's accounting as accelerator-hours per project per day. In week {{checkpoint_week}} of the quarter, projects using well below their plan return part of their allocation, which goes first to proposals on the waitlist.
sections.problem: Design the allocation system. Cover proposals and their revisions; the allocation rule as versioned code that runs on a frozen snapshot of its inputs and produces the same result whenever it is re-run; a ledger of grants, trims, returns, transfers and reserve draws; usage against allocation per project, month and accelerator type, and a forecast of each project's burn; the mid-quarter return and reallocation rule; how allocations are handed to the scheduler (as an interface; you do not design the scheduler); explanations a project lead can read ("why did I get this number?"); and the audit trail for the panel.
sections.constraints: You do not design job scheduling, queue ordering or how usage is measured; you consume daily per-project usage totals, which may arrive late or be corrected. The sum of allocations plus the reserve never exceeds the pool for any accelerator type and month. Any allocation must be reproducible from the rule version and the inputs it read. A project must not lose hours at the checkpoint because of missing usage data. Every change to an allocation records who made it and why.
sections.assumptions: Pool sizes, proposal counts, tiers, the reserve and the checkpoint rule are hypothetical and this exercise's rule; nothing here describes how any organisation allocates its compute, or its compute capacity. Accelerator types are not interchangeable unless a proposal says it can use more than one.
sections.criteria: Proposals with revisions and a frozen input snapshot; the rule as versioned, pure code whose output is reproducible from the snapshot; a ledger of grants and later changes with reasons and approvers; invariants per accelerator type and month that allocations plus reserve never exceed the pool; usage against allocation with completeness dates, so decisions use only complete data; a checkpoint rule that is explicit, protects projects from missing data, and sends returned hours to a stated destination; a reserve with one queue, visible approvals and a draw-down limit; explanations a project lead can read and re-run; a clean interface to the scheduler, distinct from scheduling and usage accounting; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the rule fixed?
clarifications.a: It is published before the quarter and versioned; changing it mid-quarter needs the panel's approval and applies only from the change forward.

clarifications.q: Can a project ask for more mid-quarter?
clarifications.a: Yes, from the reserve or from returned hours, through a short request that the system routes for approval.

clarifications.q: What counts as "well below plan" at the checkpoint?
clarifications.a: This exercise's rule: cumulative usage below 60% of the plan to date; the project keeps enough for its remaining plan plus a margin, and returns the rest. You may propose a better rule.

clarifications.q: How late can usage data be?
clarifications.a: Usually a day; during an accounting outage, up to two weeks. Corrections can change past days.

clarifications.q: Do unused hours carry over to the next quarter?
clarifications.a: No, by this exercise's rule; that is why the checkpoint exists.

hints: Freeze the inputs (the proposals at their submitted revision, the final scores, the pool per type and month, the rule version) into a snapshot with an id, run the rule as a pure function of it, and store the output with the snapshot id.

Treat every later change as an appended ledger entry with a reason (trim, return, reserve draw, transfer), so the current allocation is the initial run plus the entries, and each entry can be explained.
Checkpoint decisions should use usage data that is known to be complete through a stated date, not whatever has arrived.
followups: Walk through the allocation run at the start of a quarter, from the proposals to the numbers each project lead sees.
A project lead disputes their allocation. What does the explanation show, and can they re-run the rule themselves?
At week {{checkpoint_week}}, which projects return hours, how much, and where do the hours go? What if usage data for some projects is incomplete?
The reserve of {{reserve}} is under pressure early in the quarter. How does the system decide, and who approves?
The panel wants to know whether allocations last year matched the milestones they bought. What data answers that, and what can it never answer?

rules.ask: Two panel members edit the allocation spreadsheet the night before publication. How do you know which numbers the published allocation used?
A project lead asks why the solver gave them 12% less than last quarter. What explanation can a person read?
You hand allocations to the scheduler. What exactly crosses that interface, and what happens if a project uses more than its allocation?
Your burn forecast says a project will use only half its allocation. Do you take hours back before the checkpoint, and what if the forecast is wrong?
The rule says unused hours do not carry over. A project saved its hours for a large run in the last month. How does the checkpoint rule treat it?

incidents: The allocation run at the start of the quarter used last quarter's review scores for twelve proposals, because the input snapshot was taken before the panel's final scores were recorded. Allocations were published and two projects have already started large runs.

At the week {{checkpoint_week}} checkpoint, the return rule took hours from a project whose usage data was two weeks behind because of an outage in the accounting feed; its real usage was on plan, and its next large run is now short of hours.
The reserve of {{reserve}} of the pool was used up by week three, through urgent requests approved by four different people, none of whom could see the others' approvals.

templates.title: An evaluation result store across research teams — versioned suites, rescoring when a scorer changes, and comparisons only between comparable versions
templates.subtopic: comparability keys, per-item outputs, rescoring backfills, paired comparisons

sections.scenario: {{teams}} research teams evaluate about {{checkpoints_per_week}} model checkpoints a week against a shared catalogue of {{suites}} benchmark suites. Suites are versioned: items are added, removed when found wrong, or corrected. Scorers are versioned too: answer normalisation for exact-match suites, a sandboxed test harness for code suites, and grader models for open-ended ones. Each team runs its own evaluation harness, but every team writes its results to one shared store, and everyone reads from it: to compare two checkpoints on a suite, to follow a model family over months, and to find which results went stale when a scorer changed. Per-item model outputs are kept for {{output_days}} days so that results can be rescored without generating again. Every checkpoint, suite and score here is synthetic.
sections.problem: Design the result store. Cover what is stored per item and per run (outputs, per-item scores, aggregates), and for how long; the comparability key that decides which results may be compared; the ingestion contract that many teams' harnesses must meet, and how it is enforced; rescoring when a scorer changes, as new result versions rather than edits, with its cost and priority; the comparison API, which refuses or qualifies comparisons across incomparable versions and computes differences on the items both results share, with their uncertainty; lineage from any number on a chart back to the outputs and scorer that produced it; and storage sizing.
sections.constraints: A result is never edited in place; rescoring and corrections create new versions linked to the old. No interface may silently compare results whose suite version, scorer version, prompt template or sampling settings differ. New results are queryable within an hour of a run finishing, including while a rescoring backfill runs. Outputs older than {{output_days}} days are gone, so results that old cannot be rescored. You do not design how evaluations are scheduled or run.
sections.assumptions: Team, checkpoint and suite counts and retention are hypothetical; every result is synthetic, and nothing here describes any lab's evaluations or results. Each suite item has a stable id that survives versions unless the item's content changes.
sections.criteria: Per-item outputs and scores kept for the stated period, with aggregates derived from them; a comparability key computed from the item set, scorer, prompt template and sampling settings, stored with every result; an ingestion contract that requires those fields and rejects or quarantines runs that lack them; results immutable, with rescoring and corrections as linked new versions and superseded versions still visible; a rescoring backfill at lower priority than ingestion, with pending status shown and a clear policy for results whose outputs have expired; a comparison API that refuses or qualifies incomparable pairs and computes paired differences on shared items with counts and intervals; lineage from any number to its outputs and scorer; trend views that mark suite and scorer changes; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: What makes two results comparable?
clarifications.a: That is for you to define. At minimum the item set, the scorer, the prompt template and the sampling settings matter.

clarifications.q: Do teams use the same harness?
clarifications.a: No. Harnesses differ; some sample several outputs per item and average, others decode once. Your contract must capture that.

clarifications.q: Who decides that a scorer change needs rescoring?
clarifications.a: The suite's owners, when they publish a new scorer version. You decide how rescoring is scheduled and what readers see meanwhile.

clarifications.q: How big are suites?
clarifications.a: From a few hundred items to tens of thousands; some outputs are long programs or essays.

clarifications.q: Must old results stay visible after rescoring?
clarifications.a: Yes, as superseded versions, for anyone who cited them.

hints: Compute a comparability key from the exact item set (a hash of item ids and item versions), the scorer version, the prompt template version and the sampling settings; store it with every result and index by it.
Compare two results on the items they share, as paired per-item differences, and report the number of shared items and an interval, not just two averages.
Rescoring reads stored outputs and writes a new result version for each affected result; it runs at lower priority than ingestion, and readers can see which results are pending.
followups: Walk through one team's run landing in the store: what arrives, what is validated, and what makes it queryable.
A suite's new version removes 40 wrong items. A researcher asks to compare a checkpoint scored on the old version with one scored on the new version. What does the API return?

A scorer changes for one of the {{suites}} suites. Which results are rescored, in what order, what do readers see while it runs, and what happens to results whose outputs are older than {{output_days}} days?
Two teams report different scores for the same checkpoint on the same suite version. How does the store show why?
A chart shows a model family improving steadily over six months. How would a reader know whether any part of the trend comes from changes to suites or scorers rather than the models?

rules.ask: The two results share only 80% of their items. Do you compare the two averages, or something else, and how do you report the uncertainty?
A paper cited last month's score for this checkpoint. After rescoring, where is that number, and how does the reader see it was superseded?
A team's harness sends sampling settings as free text. What does your contract require, and what happens to a run that fails validation?
The rescoring backfill touches every result for a popular suite. How do you keep new results arriving within the hour while it runs?
Your leaderboard mixes results from three scorer versions. What does the page show, and what does it refuse to show?

incidents: A suite's version 3 removed 40 items found to have wrong reference answers. A shared dashboard compares a checkpoint scored on version 3 with one scored on version 2, and shows a two-point gain that comes entirely from the removed items.

A scorer fix for answer normalisation triggers rescoring of every result for one popular suite. The backfill competes with ingestion, new results are delayed by a day, and results older than {{output_days}} days stay on the old scorer, so the suite's long-term trend chart silently mixes both scorers.

Two teams store results for the same checkpoint and suite version under the same key, but one team's harness averages five sampled outputs per item and the other decodes once; their scores differ by three points and both are labelled as the official result.

templates.title: A public scientific database release found to contain an error after researchers have already used it
templates.subtopic: scope, correction, errata, citations and prevention

error: entries for one organism were aligned to an outdated version of their sequences, so residue numbering is shifted for a subset of them
per-residue confidence files for a batch of entries were attached to the wrong structures
a bulk archive for several organisms is missing a share of its entries, although its checksum list matches the archive as published

sections.scenario: You lead the data engineering team that builds the releases of a public database of predicted protein structures, run jointly with a partner institute that hosts the website and the API. {{weeks}} weeks after a release went live, an outside researcher emails the help address: {{error}}. Your team's first check confirms the problem and that it affects {{affected}} of the release's entries. The release has been downloaded in bulk by research groups and mirrored by other databases, and some preprints already cite entries from it.
sections.problem: What do you do? Cover the first hour, the first day and the following weeks: how you establish the exact scope; whether you correct with a new version, withdraw the affected entries, or both; what users see on the affected entry pages and in the archives; how you tell people you cannot list (downloads need no login); how you work with the partner institute on the public message; how the researcher who reported it is acknowledged; how citations to the faulty files stay resolvable and honest; and what changes so this class of error is caught before release. Then tell me about a real time you found an error in data that others had already used, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Downloads are anonymous, so you cannot contact every user. You do not know what anyone concluded from the faulty entries, and you must not speculate about biological, medical or clinical consequences. Public statements are agreed with the partner institute. Faulty files that were cited must not silently change.
sections.assumptions: The database, partner arrangement, error and figures are hypothetical; nothing here describes any real database's releases or errors.
sections.criteria: Establishes the full scope with a check that would catch the same error elsewhere before making statements; corrects through a new version, with the faulty version marked and still resolvable for citations; prepares honest errata on entry pages, release notes and archive manifests, and reaches mirrors and bulk users through the channels that exist; argues with evidence against a silent or delayed fix while agreeing the public message with the partner; acknowledges the reporter with their permission; describes impact factually without speculating about research, medical or clinical consequences; adds a release check that would have caught this class of error; real example with what they personally did and how it landed, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the error confined to one organism or batch?
clarifications.a: Your first check says so, but the check that would prove it has not run yet.

clarifications.q: Can we fix it quickly?
clarifications.a: The correct files can be regenerated in about a week.

clarifications.q: Does the partner agree on what to do?
clarifications.a: They want a quiet fix in the next scheduled release, in three months, to avoid alarming users.

clarifications.q: Has anyone else noticed?
clarifications.a: Only the reporter, as far as you know; they intend to mention it in their own paper.

hints: Scope before statements: find every affected entry with a check that would also catch the same error elsewhere.
A correction that silently replaces files breaks every citation to them; versions and an errata note keep both the fix and the record.
People you cannot list can still be reached: the entry pages, the release notes, the archive manifests, mirrors and a mailing list.
followups: What do you do in the first hour, and what do you not do yet?
The partner wants a quiet fix in three months. What do you say, and what evidence do you bring?
What exactly appears on an affected entry's page, in the archive manifest and in the release notes?
A user asks whether conclusions in their preprint are now wrong. How do you answer?
In your real example, how did people who had already used the data find out, and what changed in your checks afterwards?

rules.ask: A user publishes a result based on a faulty entry during those three months. What would you say to them, and to the reporter?
A preprint cites the faulty file. After your fix, what does that citation resolve to, and how would its reader know anything changed?
Downloads need no login. Who can you actually reach, and through which channels?
How do you describe the impact without speculating about what researchers concluded from the data?
What did you personally do in the first day?

templates.title: Researchers who want to move faster than the platform's reproducibility rules allow
templates.subtopic: understanding the cost, reducing friction, exceptions with limits

rule: every run must launch from committed code
every training data snapshot must be registered before a run may read it
every result cited outside the team must come from a run whose recipe was fully captured at launch

sections.scenario: You own the experiment platform that a research lab's teams use to launch and track runs. One of its rules is that {{rule}}; it was introduced after results could not be reproduced for a paper review. A senior researcher who leads a team of {{team_size}} asks you to waive the rule for their team until {{deadline}}. They say it costs each person an hour a day, and members of their team have started launching runs from personal workstations outside the platform, where nothing is captured.
sections.problem: How do you respond? Cover how you find out what the rule actually costs and where; what you can change in the platform quickly to reduce the cost without dropping what the rule protects; whether you grant an exception, and if so its scope, duration and conditions; how you deal with runs already happening outside the platform; who else needs to be involved; and how you would know a month later whether you made the right call. Then tell me about a real time a rule or standard you owned was slowing people down, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: You cannot remove the rule for everyone on your own; it was agreed with research leadership after the failed review. You cannot stop people running on workstations by force. The deadline is real and matters to the lab.
sections.assumptions: The team, the rule, the deadline and the figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Takes the complaint seriously and measures the actual cost before deciding, by watching the work and using platform data; separates what the rule protects from how it is enforced, and removes friction quickly where possible; grants exceptions only with scope, conditions, an end date and a plan to close the gap, or declines with reasons and an alternative; brings workstation runs back into view without blame; involves research leadership for decisions they own; defines how success will be judged later; real example with what they personally changed and what they learned, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the hour a day real?
clarifications.a: Nobody has measured it; the researcher's estimate comes from complaints on their team.

clarifications.q: What exactly is slow?
clarifications.a: Unknown. Your platform logs show launch times but not what people do before launching.

clarifications.q: Have other teams complained?
clarifications.a: Two smaller teams have mentioned the same rule, less urgently.

clarifications.q: Will the results from this push be cited outside the team?
clarifications.a: Very likely, if they are good.

hints: Watch someone work before deciding: the cost is usually in one step, not the whole rule.
Separate what the rule protects from how it is enforced today; often the protection can be kept with a lighter mechanism.
An exception needs an end date, conditions and a way to close the gap afterwards.
followups: What do you do in the first two days?
You find that most of the cost is in one step. Walk through what you would change, and how fast.
Do you grant the exception? If so, what are its terms, and what happens on the day after {{deadline}}?
Some results from workstation runs turn out to be the best ones. Can they be cited, and how do you recover their recipes?
In your real example, what did you measure, and what did you change in your own rule?

rules.ask: What exactly does the exception cover, when does it end, and how do you close the gap for runs made under it?
People are already working around the rule on workstations. What does stricter enforcement do to that?
What did you expect to find, and what would have changed your mind?
What decision do you need from leadership, and what do you bring them?
What did you personally decide, and who disagreed?

templates.title: Co-running a public resource with a partner organisation that has different priorities
templates.subtopic: shared ownership, different incentives, decisions neither side can make alone

disagreement: how often releases ship: the partner wants one fixed release a year, your side wants smaller, more frequent releases
whether to add a new kind of data file that your side can produce but the partner would have to host and support
how long old releases stay downloadable, given the partner's storage budget

sections.scenario: Your lab and {{partner}} jointly run a public database of predicted protein structures used by {{users}} of people a year. Your team builds the data; the partner hosts the website, the API and the downloads, runs user support, and answers to its own funders. The two sides now disagree about {{disagreement}}. Each side has good reasons, the working relationship has been good so far, and the next joint planning meeting is in a month.
sections.problem: How do you handle it? Cover how you understand the partner's constraints and what they are measured on; what evidence about users would help both sides; the options you would put on the table, including ones that cost your side something; how a decision gets made when neither side can decide alone; what you do if no agreement is reached by the meeting; and how you keep the relationship working while you disagree. Then tell me about a real time you worked closely with another organisation or team whose priorities differed from yours, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: The agreement between the two organisations is not yours to renegotiate. Users from many fields rely on the resource being stable. Your side cannot ship anything the partner must host without the partner's agreement.
sections.assumptions: The partner, the arrangement, the disagreement and the figures are hypothetical; nothing here describes any real partnership.
sections.criteria: Seeks to understand the partner's constraints, funders and capacity, and checks that understanding with them; gathers evidence about users that both sides trust; brings options including ones that cost their own side, such as engineering help or phased changes; uses the agreed decision path and prepares it jointly rather than escalating around the partner; keeps users' stability central and has a plan if there is no agreement; maintains the working relationship through the disagreement; real example with what they personally did and what changed in their view, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Who decides in the end?
clarifications.a: A joint steering group with members from both organisations; it meets quarterly.

clarifications.q: What do users want?
clarifications.a: There is little direct evidence: support tickets, download logs and occasional feedback at conferences.

clarifications.q: Does your side have a budget to offer?
clarifications.a: Possibly some engineering time, but money flows between the organisations only under the agreement.

clarifications.q: How does the partner's team feel?
clarifications.a: Stretched: a small team running many services.

hints: Write down the partner's constraints in their words and check them with them; disagreements often hide a cost one side does not see.
Bring evidence about users that both sides trust, collected together if possible.
Offer options that move cost to your side where you can, and make the decision path explicit.
followups: How do you learn what the partner is measured on and what the change would cost them?
What evidence would you gather before the meeting, and how would you make sure the partner trusts it?
Which options do you bring, including at least one that costs your side something?
The meeting ends without agreement. What happens next, and what do users see in the meantime?
In your real example, what did you learn about the other side that changed your position?

rules.ask: What exactly would you bring to the steering group, and how would you make sure the partner sees it first?
The agreement is not yours to change. What can you change within it?
What evidence do you have, and would the partner read it the same way?
What does the compromise cost each side, in their own terms?
What did you personally do to understand their side?

templates.title: Explaining an uncertain result to a non-specialist audience without overstating it
templates.subtopic: plain language, what is and is not known, resisting the headline

audience: a journalist writing a story due tomorrow
the board of a funding body deciding whether to renew its support
your organisation's communications team drafting a public post
result: an evaluation in which a new research model scored 1.8 points higher than the previous one on a 300-item benchmark, with an interval that includes zero (all numbers synthetic)
a predicted protein structure whose core is predicted with high confidence and whose long loops are in the lowest confidence band
a watermark detector that reports "inconclusive" for a notable share of heavily edited images in a test set the team built for testing

sections.scenario: You are asked to explain {{result}} to {{audience}}. They want one clear sentence they can use. Your team understands the result well, including what it does not show, and is worried that a simple version will be wrong in a way that matters.
sections.problem: How do you prepare and what do you say? Cover what you need to know about the audience and what they will do with the explanation; the one or two sentences you would offer, in plain words; how you explain what is known, what is uncertain and why; what you would refuse to say, and how you say no without being unhelpful; how you check what they finally publish or decide; and what you do if your explanation is later simplified into something wrong. Then tell me about a real time you explained an uncertain result to people outside your field, or say that you have not and reason it through.
sections.constraints: Every number here is synthetic. You do not draw medical, clinical or drug-discovery conclusions from a structure prediction, and you do not describe how a watermark could be removed, weakened or evaded. You cannot control what the audience finally publishes or decides.
sections.assumptions: The audience, the result and the figures are hypothetical; nothing here reports any real model's or system's performance.
sections.criteria: Learns what the audience will do with the explanation before writing it; offers a plain sentence that is accurate and useful; separates what is known, what is uncertain and what would reduce the uncertainty, using concrete comparisons rather than jargon; declines overstated wording and offers an accurate alternative; never draws medical or clinical conclusions from a prediction and never describes how a watermark could be evaded; asks to check the final text and has a plan for corrections; real example with evidence of what the audience understood, or honestly hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How much time do I have with them?
clarifications.a: Thirty minutes, and a chance to answer follow-up questions by email.

clarifications.q: Can I show a chart?
clarifications.a: Yes, one.

clarifications.q: Will I see the text before it is published or decided?
clarifications.a: Not necessarily; you can ask.

clarifications.q: Does my manager want a positive message?
clarifications.a: Your manager wants it to be accurate and understood.

hints: Start from what the audience will do with the sentence, then write the sentence that is true and still useful.
Say what the result is, what it is not, and what would make it more certain, in that order.
Uncertainty is easier to understand as a concrete comparison or range than as a statistical term.
followups: Say the one or two sentences you would offer.
They ask, "So is it better or not?" What do you answer?
They want to use a word you think overstates it. How do you respond?
Their published text simplifies your explanation into something wrong. What do you do?
In your real example, what did the audience take away, and how do you know?

rules.ask: Say that again without the statistical terms, so that someone outside the field could repeat it correctly.
Would you sign your name under that word? What would you say instead?
What can a structure prediction support, and where does your explanation stop?
How do you answer questions about defeating the detector without describing how anyone could do it?
How do you say no and still leave them with something accurate they can use?

templates.title: Project deep dive, re-examined for a research lab whose science products are public
templates.subtopic: design decisions, failures, reproducibility, public data releases and aggregate-only reporting

angle: the data model and the keys
the hardest failure you diagnosed in it
the decision you would most like to undo
requirement: any result reproducible from a recipe pinned at launch, with an honest report of what could not be pinned
a public data release in which every page, file and API response for an entry comes from one version, and old versions stay citable
aggregate outcome reporting in which no checked content is ever kept
allocations that anyone can re-derive from a stated rule and the inputs it read
scale: hundreds of thousands of experiment runs a year
hundreds of millions of public data entries
tens of millions of detection checks a day

sections.scenario: In this part of the loop you describe a data system you designed or substantially changed, one that other teams or the public depended on. The interviewer will go deep on {{angle}}, then ask how the system would have to change for a research lab whose science products are public, at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}.
sections.problem: Give a five-minute overview: the problem, the users, the scale in numbers, the architecture and your role. Then go deep on {{angle}}. Then reason through what changes at a scale of {{scale}}, with {{requirement}}. If you have never owned such a system, say so, pick the closest thing you have worked on, and be clear about which parts you are reasoning through rather than recalling.
sections.constraints: Your own project only. Describe it without revealing anything a previous employer would not want shared; round numbers are fine if you say so.
sections.assumptions: The research lab setting is hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Clear problem framing with real numbers; depth on the chosen angle down to keys, schemas and failure modes; decisions explained with alternatives and evidence; honest account of what broke and what changed; a credible re-examination that names the assumptions that would not survive the scale and addresses {{requirement}} incrementally (for example a launch-time manifest of content hashes with retention by reachability and explicit unpinned inputs; immutable version-named files with "latest" as a pointer and pages that reference versioned files; outcome records with chosen fields, content discarded in the request and minimum cells enforced at publication; a versioned rule run on a frozen snapshot of its inputs, with a ledger of later changes); own contribution clearly separated from the team's, or an honest statement of reasoning rather than recall.

clarifications.q: Does it have to be a research or machine learning system?
clarifications.a: No. Any system that moved, stored or computed data others depended on; the re-examination is where we bring it into this domain.

clarifications.q: Can it be a team project?
clarifications.a: Yes, but separate what you did from what the team did.

clarifications.q: How deep should I go?
clarifications.a: Down to keys, schemas, failure modes and numbers.

hints: Lead with the problem and the numbers before the architecture.
Have one decision you would defend again and one you would change.
For the re-examination, start from one record (a run, an entry, a check): which ids, versions and timestamps it carries, and which of them the new requirement constrains.
followups: What was the main alternative to your key design decision, and what evidence chose between them?
What broke in production, how did you find out, and what did you change?
Which parts of your design would not survive a scale of {{scale}}? What breaks first?
How would you provide {{requirement}} without a rewrite?
What would you build differently today, and why?

rules.ask: Which parts did you personally design or write?
Is that per day or in total, and what was the peak relative to the average?
Someone cited last month's version of that record. After your update, how do they find exactly what they cited?
What exactly do your logs contain, and could anything in them be content that should never have been kept?
What exactly would have to be pinned for that to be true, and which of those things did your system pin?
